On the Orders of the Day:
Is it the intention of the government to restrict the inquiry into the Home Bank affairs to the years mentioned in the order in council?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
In drafting the order in council to which the hon. gentleman refers, the government took cognizance of the petition which was presented to it by the depositors of the Home Bank. The subject matter that was referred to the commissioner is the statements that are set forth in the statement of the depositors of the Home Bank. The 44
government assumed that in referring to a commissioner allegations prepared and presented to the government by the depositors themselves, they were going as far, possibly as the depositors would think it necessary or advisable. Representations, however, have been made to the government that it might be advisable to extend the powers of the commissioner so as to include all the transactions of the Home Bank from the date mentioned down to the time of its failure, and the government intends to endow the commissioner with that power.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
The Prime Minister's
language leaves indefinite the date back to which the investigation is to go. Is the government not prepared to have the investigation go back to the issue of the charter and the reasons and justification therefor?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The government is prepared to have the fullest possible investigation made, and if in the opinion of the commissioner it is advisable to go further than has been indicated, or if in the opinion of others it seems advisable so to do, the government will be prepared to take action accordingly in the public interest.

I am prepared to give
my opinion now. I know no justification at all for limiting the investigation to special years. If a commission should be appointed to do this work, it should go back to the initial venture and have the public know all the facts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hope I made it clear that the only reason why the government made any mention whatever in the order in council of the particular years was that those are the years that are specified in the petition which the depositors presented to the government, and it was in referring that petition to the commissioner that the government had occasion to mention the years.
The public has an interest in the matter as well as the depositors.

I
would like to draw the attention of the government to the statement made by the liquidator that the Home Bank never had a banker as its manager, and I think that fact constitutes a strong argument for the investi-' gation going back to the issue of the charter.

speechtext:

Consideration of the motion of Mr. Kelly for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his Speech at the opening of the session, resumed from Monday, March 3.

Mr. Speaker, in commencing my remarks, I should like to extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Kelly) and the seconder (Mr. Lapierre) of the Address who spoke yesterday afternoon. I can congratulate the mover of the Address upon his eloquence and upon the lucidity and, on the whole, the able way in which he presented his statements. I am not, of course, acquainted with the remarks that the seconder made, but I have no doubt he filled his position just as ably and well. I can quite sympathise with a new speaker who first rises to address the House, because I can well recollect the first time I rose in this place to make a few remarks. I am free to confess that I have not yet got over the nervousness that possessed me then; and, while I do not know how long my tenure may be I am beginning to become just a little afraid that that feeling is going to stay with me. I am not at all afraid of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, nor am I afraid of gentlemen to my right, and I know I have a great many supporters behind me; nevertheless I feel a good deal of nervousness in getting up to make an address. However, I have always been treated with kindness and consideration and I have no doubt I shall receive the same considerate treatment during the short time I shall engage the attention of the House this afternoon.
I was very much pleased indeed to see that His Excellency in the Speech from the Throne tvas able to make the statement that there were signs of returning prosperity in

the affairs of our country. I doubt not that from a great many points of view this statement is true; and I am sure that every well-wisher of the country will concur in the statement I make now, that it is particularly pleasing that such should be the case at this time. I know very well that things are not as they ought to be, they are not as we would have them; but when we consider the number of Canadians who own Dominion bonds and who have savings bank deposits -which deposits have increased enormously in the last year or two-I think that we may infer from these facts, and from other conditions, that in some directions at any rate there is a returning prosperity. Unfortunately, however, this prosperity is in some respects sectional; it is evident only in some parts of the country. I am sorry to say that agriculture, the basic industry of the country, is not in a satisfactory condition. I am very well aware that world conditions have a good deal to do with the state of agriculture in Canada as well as in other countries at the present time. Nevertheless, I believe that there are certain conditions, certain disadvantages, under which agriculture is labouring to-day in this Dominion and which can be removed by proper legislation. Agriculture is perhaps in a different position from any other industry. It is our basic industry and its wellbeing affects every other calling, occupation and industry in the Dominion; and while, even with a depressed agricultural industry there may be a degree of prosperity in some particular places, in the long run the welfare and prosperity, or otherwise, of agriculture will react upon all these other occupations.
I have here a quotation which with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I shall read to the House. It is from the Montreal Gazette:
The greatest wheat crop in the history of the Dominion was produced last year. The wealth of Canada has been increased by this abundant harvest and a stimulus has been given to the revival of business. With all this, the producers in the western provinces are still dissatisfied; they are still reiterating the complaint that they are being unfairly treated, that they are compelled to buy in a dear market and sell in a cheap one. So far as the East is concerned, there is no disposition to accord the producers of the West anything less than fair treatment. The interests of the West are the interests of the Dominion.
I might add to that, that the interests of agriculture in every province of the Dominion are also the interests of the whole country. Let me read just another short extract, from an editorial article in the Montreal Daily Star.
Why do the farmers leave the West? The challenge of the West has got to be met. The immediate solvency of fills country can only be preserved by insuring

The Address-Mr. Forke
the agricultural prosperity of the West. We must make farming-grain-growing-pay in the West, and we must do it soon.
The foregoing is the language of two Montreal newspapers, and I am sure that farmers everywhere in this country will endorse it. There has been a vast amount of wealth produced in the three prairie provinces, and on the whole, throughout the Dominion, there has been prosperity, so far as production goes, for the agricultural communities. But in the case of agriculture, as in the case of every other business, the question to the man who produces is, not how much wealth he produces, but what are his net returns when he has balanced his books at the end of the year. And unfortunately, while we have had a vast stream of wealth pouring from the western prairies, it seems to me a tragedy that those who are engaged in that industry have not sufficient returns from their labours to make life comfortable or as it should be for those who produce that wealth. To make this position plain I might quote a few figures which were submitted in the Manitoba legislature by the premier of that province. Premier Bracken points out that a bushel of wheat to-day is in price only a little higher than it was in pre-war days. In 1914 you could purchase a gang plough for $84, whereas to-day it costs $153. A mower in 1914 cost $57; to-day it costs $93-as a matter of fact, I know it costs $100 at the present time. A waggon could be bought in 1914 for $111; to-day the price of a waggon is anywhere from $160 to $180. Three farm implements that could be purchased in 1914 for $253 today cost $415. Now, when -you realize that fact and remember that the price of a bushel of wheat is only just a little higher than it was a few years ago it does not require much-argument to show what position the farmer is in with respect to the raising of wheat. There are other figures too, which I might cite. In 1912, 10 fleeces from a sheep would purchase a suit of clothes; to-day it takes 31 fleeces to purchase a suit of the same quality. It is needless for me to elaborate along this line, because these figures show quite plainly just exactly the problems the farmers have to meet to-day in carrying on their industry.
We must look facts squarely in the face. I am not a pessimist; I am not going to preach blue ruin, nor do I believe that Canada is going to the dogs; I believe that there is a great future before this country and before agriculture in this country, and I hope that as the years go on we shall see agriculture in Canada occupying the place which it
deserves. If we reflect for a moment on world history we shall realize, I think, the fact that everywhere and at all times, in the case of every nation that has ever risen to prominence, whenever in a nation agriculture has begun to decay, the beginning of that nation's decay has occurred at the same time. Now, I have no idea that such a thing is likely to happen in this country. But if that be true of the nations as a whole, it is absolutely necessary that the agricultural industry in Canada should receive our very best attention.
Let me come now to the cost of doing business. I think the great complaint that wo hear at this time all over the Dominion is the high cost of production, the cost of doing business; and going from one calling to another, from one industry to another, you find always that the excuse advanced is that so much has to be charged because *he cost of doing business is so high. I would call attention to this fact. An industrial concern raises the price of its product to meet increase in costs; but the farmer to-day cannot say: I am going to charge more per bushel for my wheat because it costs me more to raise it than it did formerly. His product is sold upon the markets of the world, and consequently he has no control over its price. By reason of these conditions the farmer is at the present time at the bottom of the pyramid.
I wish I could convince everyone of the absolute necessity of placing this very important calling upon a solid basis. I know very well that, changed conditions require new methods to cope with them. We sometimes get a good deal of advice handed out to us as to how we ought to help ourselves, therefore it may be well for me to tell hon. members what some of my neighbours are doing in Manitoba. There we realize that wheat-raising is perhaps a little precarious; at the same time it must be remembered that next year and for a great many years to come wheat-raising will continue to be the greatest industry of the prairie provinces. Let me say that the return from our western wheat is gbing to be one of the principal factors in paying the public indebtedness of this country. Nevertheless we have to realize the danger of trusting entirely to a wheat crop, and our farmers are rapidly turning their attention to what is called "diversified" farming; it used to be called "mixed" farming. Last winter I had the privilege of going out to a great many meetings in Manitoba, and I may tell hon. members that politics was not so much discussed as what improvements we could make in conducting our
The Address

Mr. Forke

business so as to get better returns. I mention this so that the House may know that the farmers of the west are alive to the situation. To me one of the most hopeful signs was the entire absence of any division between town and country. We found boards of trade, agricultural societies, Canadian clubs and farmers meeting together in public in the towns and villages of Manitoba to consider our economic condition and the best methods to overcome our present difficulties.
Sometimes we are told that farmers should adopt business methods. I quite agree that they should; and if there is anything to be said in favour of income tax returns I think it is the good effect resulting from agriculturalists being obliged to sit down and figure out their operations to know exactly how they stand financially at the end of the year. The other day I received a letter from one of the most intelligent farmers in Manitoba, a man of ability and integrity, who has kept accurate accounts for the past twenty-two years. I have his figures in my room, and I once thought of putting them on Hansard, for I think they are well worth studying by the House. It is not a discouraging story, on the contrary it is a story of progress during many years, of increasing wealth in a moderate way, but during the last few years the results are very discouraging. However, I am free to .admit that on the whole the story is a very good advertisement for the province of Manitoba. I would add, Mr. Speaker, that this gentlemen has made only one great mistake in that long period-he accepted nomination at the last general election to support the party to my right.
In the Speech from the Throne the necessity of a reduction of taxation is emphasized. I think all of us are ready to say "Amen" to that statement. We all agree with it and will not in any way quarrel with the carrying out of such reduction. Sometimes we have been told that our criticism of the government last year was not severe enough. I hear that sometimes in the West. The Progressives are blamed now and then for having allowed such enormous estimates to go through without opposing them more vigorously than they did. I do not know whether anything more could have been done to reduce those estimates, but I do remember that many a speech was made from this quarter in which intimation was given to the ministers that we expected them to have [DOT]their estimates cut down very considerably this year. Now we are patiently waiting to see what they have done to cut down the expenses of carrying on the business of the 
country, in the practice of that economy which we have been promised.
The figures of the growing cost of government are so familiar to hon. members that I shall refrain from quoting them. While I do not wish to see anything done that will in any way impair the efficiency of government or in any way work injustice to anyone in connection with the enforcement of economies, I think it is perfectly evident to anyone who has given the most cursory examination to the facts of the case that something can be done and something should be done to cut down our national expenses by a very large amount. The country demands economy, but I do hope that the economy effected will be a wise economy. There is such a thing as economy that is really extravagance, and whatever work is necessary for productive enterprises I trust that that money will be found. Such works are in the nature of necessities so long as they are actual productive enterprises.
I should like to see the main estimates brought down as quickly as possible so that we may have time to study and discuss them at length. I have found from experience that it is sometimes very difficult to criticise a particular estimate through not being, familiar with the circumstances or not knowing the conditions under which the money will be expended. I rather suspect that when an estimate for a particular locality is before the House the member for the constituency in which the work is to be carried out, who knows the conditions and probably is best able to criticise the vote adversely, is not likely to take a very active part in so doing. We expect that the estimates will be cut very considerably this year to show that the business of the country is being carried on economically.
I think.it is a mistake that so many supplementary estimates should be brought down in the dying days of the session, and I for one am prepared to protest most vigorously against the practice. I remember on the very last day of last session, the last night in fact, a vast amount of money was voted that, I am sure, no hon. member, except perhaps those who were presenting the estimates, really understood or had time to consider. I have had more adverse criticism and more complaints from people who are paying attention to our proceedings of what happened the last night of last session than in regard to almost anything else that engaged our attention. So I hope that we shall not have a repetition of the bringing down of large supplementary estimates in the last moments

The Address-Mr. Forke
of the session. We can get on with our work at the beginning of the session. I am new in parliament, but it does seem strange to me that there should be so much time to spend during the early weeks and months in which we might' do business and that at the end of the session there is such a complete rush, the business being pushed through without due consideration. Let us get to work now. We are ready for our work; let us get on with the public business.
I want to say a few words in regard to the customs tariff-I suppose some hon. members have heard that phrase before; it has been a subject of endless controversy in this country and of a great deal of difference of opinion, and perhaps there is no subject that comes before the people upon which there is more confusion of thought. I do not intend to discuss it minutely or from any particular angle, but there are certain cardinal principles in connection with protection that I would just like to mention, and then pass on.
It is an accepted principle in everyday life that when you can do some particular kind of work well you make that your occupation; that is what you devote your attention to, and you are quite ready to exchange your work for that of some other man who is more interested in some other line of business. From such an exchange mutual benefit results. I submit that what is true of individuals can be equally time as between nation and nation, and that is one reason why I object to high protection as a barrier to the free interchange of goods between one country and another. Nearly four hundred million bushels of wheat will go from the West this year, most of it to find a market in the Old World. How is that wheat to be paid for? We are not going to buy anything from Europe; we are going to shut that market off; we are going to make ourselves everything that we need. Well, I would like to know what we are going to be paid with, what return we are going to get for that amount of wheat. The very a-b-c of economics will teach anyone that all trade is barter of goods, the exchange of commodities. Protection restricts markets. It cannot give employment; on the contrary, it shuts down employment. Reduce taxation by increasing the cost of living? Was any thing more absurd than the idea that by making goods dear you are going to reduce the cost of living? But why complain? Our exports last year amounted to the total of $1,028,319,123. Our imports were a great deal less-$903,-530,515. What do the worshippers at the shrine of protection want? That seems to me quite satisfactory as far as it goes. I read an
article in some magazine, written by the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and one of the questions which he asks is, how can farming be made to pay ? Of course I was very anxious to hear what anyone had to say on that subject. Well, what was the sum and substance of the whole article? Increase the tariff I So simple-no trouble; just increase the tariff and nothing but unbounded prosperity will come to agriculture and to every other industry in this Dominion of Canada, Mr. Speaker, we have had sixty years of that doctrine and we are still wondering what is going to solve our problem.
I had some quotations here that I might have read, from some speeches by hon. members to my right, in regard to the free importation of certain implements, but I shall not read them, because I think those gentlemen when they made the statements to which I refer were perfectly sincere, and they have a perfect right to change their opinions whenever they wish to do so. I might have referred to a speech made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) at Portage la Prairie, when he referred to the "ramparts of gold behind which the manufacturers were entrenched." But he also has every right to change his opinion if he wants to do so.

If the hon. gentleman will permit me, his geography is a little wrong; the speech was made in this House. At that time, however, the duty was very much higher, being under the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but-*

If the right hon. leader of the opposition would make a speech of that kind in the House. I wonder what he would have said at Portage la Prairie?
Now, I want to say a few words in connection with the stand that this group has always taken in regard to the tariff. People who are talking about the demands of the Progressive party always lay great emphasis upon articles used by the farmers. But I do not think the members on this side of the House are so much excited over farm implements; what they are interested in is the duties upon the necessities of life. We are not selfish; we want nothing but what is in the interests of this whole country from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I have some sympathy for the Canadian manufacturers; I know something about the difficulties with which they have to contend. I might make a suggestion to the government: it would not be at all amiss to take the sales tax off the price of farm implements.
The Address-Mr. Forke
And everything else.

I have no objection to taking it off all along the line, and I think that would not be a bad move, it would help the manufacturers. But I am going to make an appeal to the Canadian manufacturers of implements-I do not know whether they will listen to me or not. The Canadian manufacturer claims that he is not getting very much protection. No doubt he knows his business better than I do, but I know the feeling of the farmers and I am pretty sure that if the Canadian manufacturer of implements to-day would say, "I do not want any protection; I am going to give the farmers the benefit of free agricultural implements," such a sentiment would be created in favour of the Canadian manufacturer that he would very soon get that mass production that he says he wants. Do you know what the situation is to-day on most of the farms? I know what it is in the West and I have an idea that it is the same almost everywhere. In making up our income tax returns we are allowed ten per cent depreciation upon our implements. Do you know that . there is hardly a farmer in the West who in his tax returns to-day is allowed any depreciation on his implements?-for the reason that his implements are all over ten years old; legally they are dead and gone, out of existence, but he is still carrying on with them, doing the best he can; he is letting acreage go out of cultivation rather than buy new implements. If that sympathetic feeling could be cultivated to-day, I am sure that a vast amount of new machinery would immediately be bought, and with the mass production that would result the implement manufacturer could, I think, get along very well almost without protection.
I have no quarrel with the, Canadian manufacturer. I think the farmer and the manufacturer ought to be in the same boat; there ought to be a bond of sympathy between them, because the welfare and prosperity of the one reacts upon the welfare and prosperity of the other.
The trouble to-day is not over-production but lack of consumption. Inability to buy, that is the trouble in Canada to-day. I do not know what the Massey Harris Company, for instance, are turning out to-day, but I have no hesitation in saying that they are not turning out over one-third of the machinery they were turning out ten or fifteen years ago. Now something must be done, and something can be done, and I am sure it would be done if a proper view were taken of the situation. I am not offering this as a panacea for all ills; I am only throwing it out fMr. Forke.]
as a suggestion to the manufacturers. I knowr something about Canadian implements, and 1 know very well that the implements made in Canada are just as good as, if not better than, the implements made anywhere else in the world at the present time.
Another matter that is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne is national unity. I think that was referred to somewhat sarcastically last night, but maybe I am wrong. It seems to me this is a question on which everyone should be terribly in earnest. It is something that we ought to consider very seriously to-day. What hopes, what grand ideas we have had for the future of this Canada of ours, and at this late day are we beginning to talk of national unity? Is there any danger that East and West shall fair apart? We have heard mutterings in the West and some in the East, but I for one hope we shall hear no more of them, that that shall be a thing of the past, and that henceforth we are going to march forward as a united country seeking only the welfare and happiness of the people of this whole Dominion. But, Mr. Speaker, in the final analysis national unity must be based upon national justice. That is the only solid basis upon which we can build u?>
a great and prosperous country. Is wealth to be centralized in any particular spot in this Dominion? I for one do not want to see this a country of millionaires and paupers living side by side. I want to see it a country of moderate wealth, widely distributed over this Dominion, and no section will long continue to pay tribute to any other section of the community.
I want to say this, and I say it in all seriousness, that high protection if persisted in will not spell prosperity, but in the long run it will spell disaster for this Dominion. Somtimes the United States is pointed out as a bright and shining example of what protection has done for a country. There can be no comparison in any way between the position of Canada and the position of the United States. The United States to-day, in some of its parts, at all events, is not in just as prosperous a condition as it might be. We know that agriculture in the United States, even with its vast home market, is unable to carry.on with any great degree of prosperity.
I want to say a few words upon the question of transportation, and I have another short extract here that I want to read. It is taken from an article written by F. W. Cowie, B.A., Sc., M.E.I.C., entitled Transportation Routes in Canada and their Relation to Enduring Production. He says:
There are few subjects, at the present time, of more acute public interest, and none more vital in connection

The Address-Mr. Forke
with enduring production in Canada, than transportation routes, and the urgent demand for a reduction in the price of transportation. Tax payers look with distrust at any suggestion of a new transportation route. On the other hand ugly facts regarding production stare us in the face.
Agricultural production, in western Canada, which otherwise offers such limitless exportable resources, is reported to be in danger of not enduring, on account of profitless returns as compared with competing countries where transportation to markets, pays a lower price-
I want to draw your attention particularly to this remark because I believe it is absolutely true:
The merchant whose desk overlooks the great harbour, and whose visitors smack of the sea, is no more concerned with international trade, than the farmer a thousand miles from the seaboard.
Now if the cost of moving goods is exorbitant it simply dries up the channels of trade. It is like the hardening of the arteries in the human body. It simply means that in the not far distant future the whole course of business will come to an end. Reduction in the cost of transportation is an absolute necessity in this country. Sometimes a thing may be an absolute necessity and yet not be within the bounds of probability. However, I do hope that there may be some method and some way adopted whereby we can reduce the cost of transportation, because I believe that upon the solving of this problem the future prosperity of our country to a very large degree depends. We want the shortest and the cheapest routes to be utilized. We sometimes speak about our Canadian [DOT]harbours. I want to see all the trade possible brought to our Canadian harbours. I want to see every harbour used to the extent that it is possible to use it with economy and to the best advantage.
I want to say a few words about the Hudson Bay railway. I know a great many gentlemen in this House are anxious to get a little more information in regard to this very much needed enterprise. In fact, I know that two members in this part of the House have taken the trouble during the recess to go over the Hudson Bay route, examining the condition of the roadbed., viewing the harbour and all the improvements that have been made up there, and if we seem a little exuberant in this part of the House over the building of the Hudson Bay railway, give us credit at least for trying to get all the information we possibly can upon this undertaking. I hope one of these gentlemen at least, and perhaps both of them, will tell the House what they saw and the condition of things generally in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. They came
back with a fine story, that there was a grand country up north, that it was well worth building a railroad into if for no other purpose than colonization, that there was great wealth up in that northern country. All over t.hei west during this last year there have been meetings held by boards of trade and resolutions passed by agricultural societies and other bodies. In the city of Winnipeg we have organized to-day a "Build the Hudson Bay road" society. I want the government and hon. members of this House to understand that not for one moment can this subject be downed, because the West is determined to have the Hudson Bay railway built, and it will be built, I believe, in the not far distant future. Bear in mind that a great many people have expressed a well-founded opinion on the feasibility of this route. For over three hundred years the ships of the Hudson's Bay Company were passing in and out of that harbour, and they had very, very few accidents in all those years. However, I think this subject will be dealt with at another time.
Another matter that is mentioned in the Speech from the Throne is the satisfactory showing made by the Canadian National Railways and the progress they have made during the past year. I think every lover of our country must rejoice in the fact that we see these roads on the way to prosperity. Year by year the conditions are improving and in the not very far distant future I believe we are going to have a valuable system of railways in this country in the possession of the people.
There is an idea, and it is not original with me-it has been mentioned quite frequently in this House-and that is that the overcapitalization of the National Railways ought to be written off and a re-valuation made, which would represent the actual value of the road, and in that way the Board of Management would be given an opportunity to show what could be done under government ownership of railways. At the present time the railways are loaded with money that was misspent, money that might just as well have been thrown into the sea. That expenditure was a national loss and the nation will have to stand that loss ultimately anyway, and it seems to me it would be good business to write down that over-capitalization to a figure that the railways actually represent. That would encourage the Board of Management and the people, and perhaps make it possible in the not far distant future to have a drastic cut in freight rates over the roads. I would like to say in connection with the Board of
The Address-Mr. Forke

Management that sometimes we see criticism of the board, but I think everyone who wishes well for these railways was agreed that the Board of Management ought to have a free hand, without any political manipulation or influence over them, to show what they could do and to see whether it was possible to make of that system a paying proposition. It seems to me that the Board of Management have done well. I think they have done just as well as could be expected under the conditions. That they have made mistakes, no one can deny. It is very human to make mistakes, and is there anyone in this House who is able to cast the first stone? So I do hope from this on that all political manoeuvring and party advantage will be lost sight of in connection with the railways, and that every member of this House will be anxious to see that the Board of Management and the Canadian National Railways are given a fair chance. I do not suggest that they are not getting a fair chance. I hope they are, but I can assure you, Mr Speaker, that the country will not stand for anything that will jeopardize the future welfare of this great enterprise. I sometimes think there might be something done in the way of a committee composed of members of all parties in this House who could perhaps take under their peculiar care matters affecting the Canadian National Railways- anything in the world to prevent the railways from being made a partisan matter on the floor of this House, anything that will get parliament working harmoniously together to see that the railways prosper.
Now just a word in regard to freight rates on the Great Lakes. We are told that provision is to be made that freight will be carried at the very lowest rate from the Great Lakes to the ocean, and from the ocean to Liverpool. When I think of the conditions last fall and what took place on the Great Lakes, it does not fill me with very much pride. I think that Canadians as a whole might rather feel humiliated over what happened on the Great Lakes last fall, and no matter what part of the House hon. gentlemen may sit in, I think the conditions reflected equally upon the whole parliament of this country. Now, let me say a word or two m connection with the subject of ocean freights. There can be, and there ought to be, steps taken to prevent any such unfortunate position as that. Surely enough ships can be found in Europe to transport our cattle at reasonable rates. A word or two now in regard to immigration. I know that my own opinions on this question do not exactly coincide with the views of some of the members even on my own side of the House. Nevertheless I feel impelled to make this statement: I do not for one moment think that putting up the bars against imports and then pulling them down in some other place, or letting in immigrants indiscriminately is going to solve our present difficulties. At the same time I do believe that a sane policy of immigration would have that happy result in the case of a great many of our troubles. I shall not rehearse the rather depressing story about the numbers of people that are leaving this country and crossing to the other side. Mr. Speaker, so long as Canadians live beside a nation which numbers one hundred and ten millions there will be, at all times, a certain drift of people into the United States. The attraction which numbers holds out, the operation of the law of gravitation, will have its influence and there will always be a movement of that kind to a greater or lesser extent. As to the question "Who goes to the United States?" let me say this: I had the privilege after the last session of parliament of visiting the city of Kingston and speaking there to the students of Queens University. I had the pleasure of attending the banquet of the graduating class of that year. I looked at that splendid gathering of young men and young women, bright, intelligent-oh! nothing finer in this Dominion-and the thought came into my mind, "Here are perhaps, a hundred young men and women of whom fifty per cent may cross the line in a very short time to seek an outlet for their energies, for their abilities, and for their education." That this seems to be the case is, to me, one of the tragedies of the present situation. I do not know just how we can cope with such a situation, but every attempt should be made to render conditions in Canada as attractive as possible in order that young people of that fine character may be induced to remain in their native land. I have often thought that if we could get some
young men with intelligence, with education, [DOT] and with initiative power out into our farming districts of the West to take up agriculture there as their life work, it would be a great blessing and a great advantage to that community. Unfortunately we do not find them there; the conditions are not such at the present time as to attract anybody who has any ambition whatever. '"Who comes and who goes?" I am afraid sometimes we are losing a very fine type of people. I am not blaming the government for this, I am not blaming anyone; I am looking conditions in the face and trying to find a remedy for them.
I have spoken of those who go. Now as to those who come. I have already said that I do not want to see a policy of indiscriminate immigration adopted. Do you know that in the three western prairie provinces the Anglo-Saxon people-and you might include with them those of the French race-are in the minority? Whatever the future of those provinces may be, the population is not going to be of Anglo-Saxon or of French descent; it is going to be something we know not what, and we want to be careful how we start out with foreign stock. I am not at all afraid, but we have at the present time just about enough to absorb of that description in our western prairie provinces. By all means, let us have immigration-immigration of the right sort. Get me young men, young women also, healthy and willing to work, coming from Great Britain, Scandinavia, France. I would not be afraid of Germans either at this time. They are all right; they will make good citizens in time. I will take all the immigration of that kind we can possibly get. The first thing we want to be careful about is to make conditions suitable for the people when they come here. Taxation is one of our problems; transportation is another, and the doubling of our population would go a long way towards solving those two problems. Conditions may not be just what they ought to be in Canada; but when w.e think of the
2,000,000 unemployed people in the British Isles to-day, we should not be afraid of inviting them here to work. Canada is all right; our country is as good as it ever was; we have just as much faith in it as we ever had, and notwithstanding the present difficulties which we are encountering, I have no fear at all for the future of our country.

It is very significant indeed that the last speaker (Mr. Forke), the leader of the Progressive party in this House, should have closed his speech with a quotation from the Prime Minister of Great Britain. It proposes:
To secure for the producers, by hand or by brain, the full fruits of their industry and the most equitable distribution thereof that may be possible upon the basis of the common ownership of the means of production, and the best obtainable system of popular administration, and control of each industry or service;
to co-operate with the labour and socialist organ-1 izations in the dominions and the dependencies with a view to promoting the purposes of the party, and to take common action for the promotion of a higher standard of social and economic life for the working population of the respective countries;

I desire to call attention to a paragraph or so taken from the manifesto which was issued to the people of Great Britain. I do so because I believe that the attitude of the present

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
government of Great Britain will have its very decided effects upon the policies of the various Dominions.
The Labour party challenges the tariff policy and the whole conception of economic relations underlying it. Tariffs are not a remedy for unemployment; they are an impediment to the free interchange of goods and services upon which civilized society rests. They foster a spirit of profiteering, materialism and selfishness, poison the life of nations, lead to corruption in politics, promote trusts and monopolies, and impoverish the people. They perpetuate inequalites in the distribution of the world's wealth, won by the labour of hands and brain. These inequalities the Labour party means to remove.
The Labour party proposes to restore to the people their lost rights in the land, including minerals, and to that end will work for re-equipping the Land Valuation Department, securing to the community the economic rent of land and facilitating the acquisition of land for public use.
The Labour party is working for the creation of a commonwealth of co-operative service. It believes that so far only a beginning has been made in the scientific organization of industry. It will apply in a practical spirit the principle of public ownership and control to the mines, the railway service and the electrical power stations, and the development of municipal services.
Labour's vision of an ordered world embraces the nations now torn with enmity and strife. It stands therefore for a policy of international co-operation, through a strengthened and enlarged League of Nations, the settlement of disputes by conciliations and judicial arbitration, the immediate calling by the British government of an international conference, including Germany, on terms of equality to deal with the Versailles Treaty, especially reparations and debts, and the resumption of free economic and diplomatic relations with Russia. This will pave the way for disarmament, the only security for the nations.
I think perhaps that members of this House will be in a better position to judge of the arguments and policies which we attempt from time to time to put forth in this comer of the House, if they understand that we have been working very much along the lines proposed by the Labour party of Great Britain cooperating with the international organizations of which it forms a unit.
Before I speak to the more general questions relative to economic conditions in Canada, I propose to introduce a particular matter which has been of very great concern to our working class population. I refer to the situation in Nova Scotia among the miners and steel workers. A commission has recently reported ' on the conditions there, but the Speech from the Throne contains no intimation whatever that any definite action is contemplated. We had a royal commission in 1920, we have had boards of inquiry and conciliation, we have had special inquiries, we have had the military sent down to that province twice within the last two years, and yet the conditions remain, if anything more unsatisfactory than ever. I say this in full view of the fact that recently the miners have returned to work. These inquiries and commissions have revealed wretched housing and sanitary conditions,

abuses connected with the company's stores, unsatisfactory working conditions, low wages and irregular work, and in the case of the steel workers long working days of eleven and thirteen hour shifts, with every other week twenty-four hours on end. These unsatisfactory conditions prevail notwithstanding the fact that Canada was a signatory of the Peace treaty under which the workers were supposed to be given an eight hour day.
The employees have been investigated. I would suggest that it is about time that the employers, the British Empire Steel Corporation, should be'investigated, and I would urge upon the government the appointment of a parliamentary committee that would go fully into these conditions which have been causing so much trouble to the authorities and such hardship to a considerable section of our people. This committee might very well investigate the abnormal profits of the corporation during the war, government contracts and subsidies, the absentee management with its officials alleged to be incompetent and superabundant, the fact that real costs and profits have often been concealed through contracts between constituent and subsidiary companies, and the amount of watered stock in the corporation.
About a year ago there appeared in the Toronto Star a series of articles dealing with the situation in Nova Scotia. One or two excerpts which suggest that the real investments of this company are not sufficient to warrant the large profits that the management insist upon taking out of the business may be of interest to hon. members. The writer says that the promoter in the first instance:
-estimated the cost of his plant at $6,000,000 at the outside. He then bonded it for that amount; and on top of that issued $15,000,000 in common stock. This original $15,000,000 of common "watered" stock is represented in the existing issues of Besco stock by $6,000,000 of common stock and by $13,500,000 of seven per cent second preference, on which the dividends are accumulative liability.
That was in the early days.

I venture to quote a paragraph or two from a recent book by Viscount Milner, The Questions of the Hour:
The real gravamen of the charge against our present industrial system is not that it involves an unfair distribution of the product, but that it mismanages, misdirects and therefore unduly limits production itself.
Such results are inevitable as long as the investment of capital, determining as it does the nature and distribution of employment, is governed wholly by considerations of individual gain.
They (the wage earners) have nothing whatever to say as to the direction of capital, upon which their employment depends, yet they may at any moment be reduced to penury by its misdirection.

In my own

If that principle is to be put into practice we shall have an extension instead of a lessening of the income tax, we shall have the 5 p.m. establishment of an inheritance tax, we shall have the adoption of a tax on land values and the values of other natural resources thus giving the people more ready access to these.
We are told that there are to be certain tariff re-adjustments. Just what these are I do not know, but I would suggest that the tariff re-adjustments must be accompanied by other measures, or their results may prove disastrous. It may very well be, if the privileges of certain industries are taken away from them without other corresponding changes in our system, that there will result very great hardship indeed. We all recognize that manufacturing in this country is difficult because of the high overhead charges, including all kinds of inflation, and because of the taxation and the high cost of living. What we need to do to-day is to adopt some system by which these costs may be lessened and industry may be able to go free. In fact I have sometimes thought that the greatest financial need of to-day is the raising of the mortgages that press so heavily upon industry of every description. I wish we had something in the nature of what we are told about in the Old Testament, the establishment of a year of jubilee when the slaves and the debtors could go free. If that could be brought about once I am sure there would be prosperity in Canada.

May I quote a
sentence or two in this connection from the report of the ordinary general meeting of the shareholders of the Midland Bank Limited, as reported in the London Times of January 26, 1924. The Right Hon. Reginald McKenna said on that occasion:
When national output is below productive capacity the policy should be to let money out: When production is at a maximum, the outflow of money should be checked, and if inflationary symptoms have appeared money should be withdrawn.
We have deliberately to make up our minds as to what we want.
If we mean to get rid of unemployment we must have more money in existence to take up the increased production.
This, of course, refers particularly to bank policy, but it is equally true of a government policy in dealing with financial affairs. As Mr. J. A. Hobson maintains in The Economics of Unemployment:
The proper provision against trade depressions and unemployment lies in strengthening the consuming powers of the community, so that effective demand for consumable goods may keep full pace with every increased productivity that arises from improvements in the arts of industry; and the strengthening of consumption is obtained by a better distribution of the product of industry.
The Speech from the Throne makes incidental reference to the Home Bank, and there is to be provision, we are told, for the appointment of a commission. May I ask the question that has been asked very generally across Canada-Why not an investigation by parliament itself? Perhaps we on this side of the House are apt to feel just now that no group was more speedily justified than those of us who last year attempted to secure greater security for the shareholders and depositors of the banks. It was stated
that there was no need for the adoption of an amendment which I myself put forward, that there should be government auditors. If I remember aright the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) told us that he had consulted with the bankers and that they did not consider government auditors necessary. We feel further that we were quite justified in asking that there should be a full investigation into the whole of the credit system. We trust that the recommendations of last year's committee will be carried out this year.
In closing, since it is very difficult for a small group such as we are, through the motions and amendments which are brought forward adequately to express what our viewpoint really is, I venture to summarise very briefly.
In view of the enormous national debt with its heavy interest charges; of the high taxation, much of which results in the transference of wealth from the many to the few; of the burden of overhead charges which is crippling industry and commerce; of the deplorable condition of agriculture owing largely to tariffs, high freight rates and inadequate credit facilities; of unemployment resulting from a lack of purchasing power sufficient to absorb production; of the continued emigration of our people; of the instability of our banks as revealed in recent mergers and failures; of the concentration of economic power in the hands of a small group who are able to direct the policy of industry for their own financial gain, rather than toward supplying human needs:
And also in view of the fact that Canada possesses abundant natural resources; sufficient plant equipment-now working below capacity-to convert our raw material into consumable commodities; a plentiful supply of labour to man the plant equipment; and ample national credit-based on our national resources and the productive power of our people-more than sufficient to finance every necessary industrial and commercial enterprise :
We urge that during the present session of parliament steps should be taken towards:
(a)	the establishment of a proper system of taxation by which our natural resources will be made more readily available for the use of the people:
(b)	the operation under co-operative and democratic management of our plant equipment, thus providing more abundantly for the needs of the people:
(c)	reforms, or reorganization, in our financial system by means of which more equitable distribution may be secured:

(d)	the basing of our foreign trade policy and international relations on the clear recognition that the world has become an economic unit in which the welfare of each nation is dependent upon the welfare of all others.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend at this time of the afternoon to follow the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) in his remarks concerning labour conditions in England, labour conditions in Nova Scotia, and those prevailing in the different cities in Canada. My attention was drawn somewhat to conditions prevailing in the cities of Montreal and Toronto and other places near Ottawa where we have some knowledge of what is taking place at the present time. He complains that in those large cities there is unemployment during the winter season. That has been one of the drawbacks of Canada since Canada has been in existence. We have seasonal occupation. In Montreal, with which I am familiar, as I have lived there most of my life, every fall and early winter there is an invasion of people from the country districts who have been engaged during the summer in navigation, in farming, railway construction and so on, and who enter the city for the purpose of wintering there. That condition has prevailed at all times. It prevails in Winnipeg; it prevails in Ottawa; and .it will prevail generally throughout Canada until we find seasonal occupations during the winter season. An attempt has been made in that respect through the western country, and from what I have been able to gather, I understand that it has met with a measure of success. In Montreal, at the present time, the building trades are occupied with trying to solve that problem of carrying on building operations during the whole of the winter so as to prevent those large numbers of workmen from being unemployed during the winter season. That is one matter which will have to be solved with time and with the experience which has been gained. No government can be blamed for that condition of affairs, no more than can any government be blamed for the emigration of Canadians to the United States.
This is my twenty-fifth session of parliament that I am beginning now and I have heard that discussed over and over again at all times. I have more particular knowledge of the province of Quebec, where I was born and brought up than of any other part of Canada, and I well remember away back fifty years ago when I was a mere boy, that

farm houses in the valley of the Richelieu, farm houses in the valley of the St. Lawrence were closed for one, two, three years while the farmer left with his family to enter the manufacturing towns of the New England states, to make up for what he was unable to extract from his farm. They went there by the thousands. I believe to-day [DOT] there are not less than 2,000,000 Canadians, three-quarters of them of French-Canadian origin, who now inhabit the eastern states. In some cities they have almost a majority. They have elected lieutenant governors. They have elected mayors of cities. The late Curtis Guild, a former governor of Massachusetts, told me twenty years ago when I was honoured by the Canadian Club of Boston by being asked to deliver an address there, that at that time there were enough Canadians and descendants of Canadians, mostly from the Maritime provinces, to control the election of the mayor of Boston. Therefore, this exodus from Canada to the United States has existed at all times. It has been accentuated during the last year or two because of the industrial boom which has taken place in the United States and with which all readers of the newspapers are familiar. Higher wages attract the workmen especially during the [winter season when unemployment is the rule in Canada, and they go from all parts of Canada to the United States. From my own constituency a stream of young men left for Detroit to work in the automobile factories there. Some of them made a success of their trip; others were there for a time; but the majority of them have come back, because there is a lure of the home land which cannot be found elsewhere. The great drawback, however, of Canada is that we have lost many valuable sons and daughters who have gone to other lands, chiefly to the United States, and whom we should have kept here. But as the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) has said, as long as the United States remains as it is, it is impossible to believe that the day will ever come when that great magnet will not be an attraction for Canadians. The only solution for that problem which we have is to try to keep our people at home by giving them employment here, realising that a Canadian is a man who is born or brought up	in
this country and who is enamoured of the country and that a Canadian is worth

two men who come from the outside.
I heard the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) a moment ago refer to immigration in the West. Immigration is not a burning issue in my constituency nor was it ever of any great consequence there. The same is true, Mr. Speaker, of the constituency you represent. Both you and I, Sir, represent in this House-you have done so for almost thirty years and I for nearly a quarter of a century-the oldest part of the province of Quebec, that spot where Jacques Cartier landed before he ascended the St. Lawrence and proceeded ultimately to Quebec and Montreal. That part of the province of Quebec, the Gaspesian peninsula, comprises some ten thousand square miles, the size of an ordinary kingdom or two of Europe, and it has never been the centre of attraction for immigrants. They all pass by the shores of Gaspe and ascend the St. Lawrence, going on to Ontario and the West. The Gaspe country, I say, has no attractions for settlers coming from Europe. An attempt was made some years ago by the provincial government to establish some Belgian farmers in the backwoods of St. Charles de Caplan in my constituency, but the poor people who came in almost perished the first winter. They all departed in the following spring. No; we shall never have immigration into the Gaspe peninsula because the people who make a success of life there are the rugged woodsmen and fishermen, who are to the manner bom; they are indigenous to the soil, so to speak, and can stand a temperature of 25 or 30 degrees below zero. They spend the winter in their lumber shanties and with their. axe hew out such farm land as is necessary for the young settler and his family. That is the class of people who inhabit that country; they do not come from Europe and they never will. Those immigrants who come to Canada from Europe are attracted to the fertile fields of the western plains, where they are told that in a year or two there is a crop awaiting them. I do not blame them because I know that the same attraction exists for the Americans who come across the border.
We have had problems discussed in this House, some of which I am sorry to say have not been solved to this day; but others have been solved by the common sense of the Canadian people, because under our form of government there is a solution for every grievance no matter what its nature may be. We have difficulties at the present time, and one of the outstanding difficulties is the paucity of the population as compared with the great burden we have to bear as a result of our participation
in the war. It was my good fortune when commissioner of Montreal three or four years ago to receive, along with my colleagues, that eminent man who played such a great part in the world war, Cardinal Mercier. His visit was a very transient one; he was merely passing through the country on his way elsewhere. He was not as familiar with Canadian conditions as we should have liked him to be, because his visit was originally intended for the United States. But when we told him of the extent of the participation of our Canadian people in the world war he was amazed to learn that 600,000 Canadians had gone overseas and that this country had incurred a debt which was truly bewildering. The distinguished -prelate could hardly conceal his astonishment at learning the extent to which we had gone into the war.
Now that things have calmed down and the events of that time have passed into history, and many of those who participated in the debates then have disappeared from the scene, we may admit that we probably overdid matters in the war in our enthusiasm to do our share. We probably sent to the other side many men who should not have been sent, many who were unfit for the trenches, many who were unable to do the work which they were called upon to do. We probably incurred a great deal of indebtedness which we could have avoided if we had had the wisdom we now have. In one of the last speeches of the late Minister of Militia, who was so energetic in organising the first and second contingents to Europe, that gentleman declared that every dollar spent in the war was wasted, because war was waste from beginning to end. However that may be, we have to face the conditions to-day and we must bear them.
There is no man who is familiar with the state of affairs in this country at the present time, who knows its natural resources and knows the spirit of the people, who doubts for a moment that Canada will meet all her obligations. The Canadian dollar stands at par in the markets of the world; it stands practically so in New York; and this is a matter for gratification when we remember that the countries of Europe have witnessed the depreciation of their currency to the extent that we have seen.
The solution we must find is to do away with any misunderstanding which may exist, as some have said, between western and eastern Canada. I was glad to hear the leader of the Progressive party declare that so far as he knew there was no reason why there should be any cleavage between the two great portions of this count.rv. The salvation

of this Dominion lies in a united Canada. We may have differences of opinion; we may kneel at different shrines; we may speak different languages. But our aim should be one, the union of our people and the building-up in this North American continent of a great nation equal to the ones from which we have sprung. I heard the hon. member say that in some provinces of the West the people of British stock, together with the French Canadians,-because after all they are practically Britishers too, equal to if indeed not better than some Britishers-find themselves to-day in the minority in the West amongst the people who have come from other countries. That is a matter which the government cannot very well overlook. It should make certain that at all times there is a majority of people in this country who have been brought up under British institutions and who can be assimilated into Canadian citizenship.
The House was no doubt pleased, as I am sure the country was, to learn from the lips of the Prime Minister, (Mr. Mackenzie King) of the great improvement which has taken place in our finances, in business and in transportation, and in matters generally of common interest to the country. Now, two years and a few months is a very brief period for a new administration to undertake to put its house in order after the country has passed through such an ordeal as this country experienced from 1914 to 1921. True, the war ended in 1918; but the three years that followed, with demobilization and the responsibilities which were imposed upon the country, was a terrible ordeal for a country, and this government accepted a heritage such as was never bequeathed to any other administration. The leader of the Progressive party said a moment ago that the government found itself in the minority at the present time. Well, the leader of the opposition, (Mr. Meighen) did not care to put that question to the test. So far as we have gone I have reason to believe that if the Speech from the Throne is adopted, and I have no doubt that it will be, if the broad lines therein laid down are followed out, this government is no longer in a minority; far from it, it will have an overwhelming majority in the House, because the Speech from the Throne appeals to the common sense, the patriotism and the honesty of every hon. member. We all have in view the betterment of the country's finances and the solution of our railway difficulties; we desire to see an improvement in the transportation

problem and an increase in our population, together with a stabilization of finance. These are all questions on which we can agree. We may differ as to the methods by which they are to be settled, but undoubtedly we all have these things as a part of our aim in the fulfilment of our duty.
I must congratulate the government, and I know the great majority of this House will do the same, upon having realized the great responsibility placed upon it and that economy -not economy, as we might say, in the stopping of productive expenditure, but economy in stopping waste, no matter where it exists -is about to be introduced. This is absolutely necessary in the present condition of the country.
Our exports and our imports are increasing, our business generally is good. The feeling between the West and the East is improving. Changes have been hinted at in the tariff, The Canadian government is composed of men who are familiar with the various conditions prevailing in Canadian industry today, and we may depend upon them to see that any change made in the tariff will be such as will benefit the whole country, and that no deliberate step will be taken to wound or fatally destroy any of our industries which have a reason to exist. Changes in the tariff have to be made carefully after proper consideration, and if they are brought about, as they should be, in the interests of the whole people, they will be accepted as such, because manufacturers as well as farmers must take the sweet and the sour; they cannot expect that tariffs will always be favourable to their views.
The hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) has spoken of the conditions prevailing in some communities, in the course of which he referred to the overhead charges and the long hours of labour, but I did not hear him make any reference to the high wages prevailing in some of our cities. The manufacturer says that these high wages are a drawback to him in meeting the competition of the American and the English manufacturer. He claims he is paying higher wages than are paid in some parts of the United States, but more especially higher wages than are paid in Great Britain. I would be the last man in this House to advocate the reduction of the wages of a working man, because I am somewhat familiar, having lived for many years in a large city, with the conditions he has to put up with, especially if he is rearing a large family, and this has been the rule rather than the excep-

tion in our province. Therefore I would be the last man to take away a farthing from a working man who is bringing up a family. On the other hand, it might be good policy to ask working men, who are more familiar with their own conditions than we can expect to be, whether very high wages naturally and necessarily mean prosperity for them. If the cost of living is to increase in consequence of the high wages that are being paid, where is the advantage to the working men? Would it not be better to make a gradual readjustment, in the course of which wages would be reduced as well as the cost of living? We all remember when Canadians used to work for $1.50 a day. When I was a boy running around the lobbies of the old House the men across the river in the Booth and the Eddy mills used to work for $1, $1.25 and $1.50 a day of ten hours, and they were perfectly happy and just as prosperous as their successors to-day who are earning from $4 to $8 a day. We have heard a great deal from the West. Other members will speak for their sections of the country; it is my right and duty, Mr. Speaker, to refer more particularly to my own constituency. In so doing I am sorry that I must bring up an issue which I have discussed many times in this House. In the Gaspe peninsula transportation is the great question, as it is in western Canada, and as it is no doubt in other parts of the Dominion. Lately a Roman Catholic bishop has been appointed to the See of Gaspe, which has one of the finest seaports in North America. I am referring to Monseigneur Ross, whose grandfather was a Scotchman, tout who met the fate that all Scotchmen meet when they marry French Canadian women. He gave up the Gaelic language and started to speak French. He is a young but distinguished man and has undertaken to give the Gaspe peninsula some of the many things which it is lacking. One of these is education, another is the development of that part of the province of Quebec. He has been seconded in his efforts very heajtily by the government of the province in so far as
their jurisdiction extends to the improvements he has in view. He is building a seminary there, he is building schools, and at the present time he is negotiating with the Trappist Fathers-at Oka to establish an industrial school so as to extend to the Gaspe people the benefits of agricultural instruction. But he has told you, Mr. Speaker, and he has told me, and he has told the people publicly, and he has told Sir Henry Thornton at a meeting to which I shall refer in a moment, that all this work will be in vain if the railway situation in that country is not brought to a solution. I know the attitude taken by the present government, that the railways are out of their control, having been handed over to the management of Sir Henry Thornton and a board of directors. I with the majority in this House voted for the placing of the National Railways in the hands of a commission having at its head a distinguished man; and Canadians today are familiar enough with Sir Henry Thornton to know that he is a distinguished man in every respect, and that we have been very fortunate in securing his services.
When the question of bringing about _ a change in the railway situation in our district became acute, I suggested to Monseigneur Ross that the best thing would be to bring Sir Henry Thornton into the constituency in order that he might become familiar with the people and the natural resources and he came on your invitation, Mr. Speaker. The Gaspe peninsula is not on the main line of travel. If it were it would be to-day one of the finest strategical points in the Dominion. As you go to the Maritime provinces you cross the Restigouche river at Matapedia and the Gaspe peninsula is left on one side. But one day the construction of a railway was undertaken on the Gaspe coast. I realize in making this report that it is not part of my official duties as Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, but, having given the matter a good deal of personal consideration, I feel I am not overstepping the bounds of propriety in giving you my personal views on such an important subject.
I will leave the matter there, Mr. Speaker. It is close to six o'clock and I do not want to impose upon the House the necessity of listening to a minute description of all the resources we have in that peninsula-ten thousand square miles of what is practically "terra incognita," merely the shore line inhabited, but inhabited by seventy thousand rugged people, the descendants of the pioneer settlers of that part of the country, many from Great Britain, others from France, and others from other parts of the province of Quebec. We ask for these people fair treatment. We ask that they be given an opportunity to eke out a living in that part of Canada to which they have stuck so long and so faithfully. Nothing is more painful to you, Mr. Speaker and to myself, than to see these people emigrating to the American cities or to other parts of Canada-they who live in one of the most fertile parts of the province of Quebec, blessed with a double crop, the crop of the sea and the crop of the land, with lumber and minerals galore. We have discovered recently in the township of Lemieux, in the county of Gaspe, four square miles of lead and zinc which are declared by the experts of the Mines department to be superior to the famous Joplin deposits in the state of Missouri.
