Mr. Speaker, just before the House took recess I listened to the remarks of the hon. member for Bona venture (Mr. Marcil) in regard to the railway difficulties that confront his constituency on the Baie de Chaleur. I agree with a good deal of what he says. I am somewhat conversant with the need of railways in that part of the province of Quebec. I know the hardships which the people there have to 
encounter by reason of the existing situation, and I would like to see some relief accorded to them. I do not know that this should come altogether through a steam railway, perhaps the needs of the people would be better served by an electric line; but if the board of directors of the National Railways would take the matter up in a businesslike way and work out the solution somewhat in the manner I have suggested, a railway service might be provided which would help the people of Bona-venture out of their difficulties. They have had a hard time, but they have a fine district down there and they have hope and faith in their country. I should like to see that part of Canada developed equally with other portions which we hope to see ultimately developed and become a great source of benefit to Canada.
Having said that much I am going to take up the time of the House for a little While to-night to discuss two or three questions which I think are of supreme importance to Canada. To begin with, I want to point out to Canadians, and especially to the voters of the Dominion, that the greatest political revolution that has occurred within the past one hundred years is now taking place in every country that has a political system similar to that which we have in the British dominions and that they have in the United States; and the best way to illustrate that revolution is to tell the House what has taken place.
First of all I am going to describe what has taken place in Canada. In 1919 in the province of Ontario the Farmers' party began to organize themselves. They did organize themselves and an election came on. The other parties neglected even to have conventions to discuss the situation, and the result was that this Farmers' party that everybody despised came into office and was there for some time. So much for that. Then, in 1921, Union government ceased to be a factor in Canada. It was dissolved and my right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) who now leads the opposition became Prime Minister. He decided that he would ask His Excellency for a dissolution of parliament. His request was granted. He went to the country and came back absolutely in a minority. The Liberals assumed office with a small majority, and out of that came change. But before I go into that I want to refer to another election, that of Mr. Drury in the province of Ontario. He was premier then. He had not been premier and did not hold any office at the time of the previous election. He decided also to go the country. He did so and was not only defeated but his party was almost

The Address-Mr. Maclean {York)
destroyed. The Conservative government then assumed office in Ontario, and that government now administers the affairs of the province. Then there was another election in 1923 in the Mother country. They had abandoned the Union government there a short time before Bonar Law became Prime Minister. Unfortunately he died. The party elected a new leader in Stanley Baldwin, who occupied office for a time when he decided he would go to the country for a mandate. He went to the country for a mandate and he came back without a majority. Labour, a new party came into office and assumed the government, and they are administering it to-day. They are also in a minority, and yet they occupy the Treasury benches. This came about because the leader of that party had the wit when the opportunity came to assume the leadership of the opposition. There was nothing else to do, by reason of what took place, but to have Ramsay MacDonald come into office although his party was in a minority. At any rate, to-day the Conservatives are out of office and the Liberals are weakened. The latter came back divided but since then they have united. Well, this is the outstanding feature of all these elections -that the political revolution has come, and it extends all over the British Dominions, and it has also come to our neighbours in the United States. Out of these elections we have these various parties in Ontario. We still have the Farmers' party, we still have the Liberal party, and we have the Conservative party. Those three are playing the triangle; they are still there to-day. Here in Ottawa, after the last general election, the Liberals came back with a majority. We do not know what they had a few days ago but they are confident now. Thus we have in this House a Conservative party, a Liberal party in office, a Farmers' party, and a Labor party; and instead of playing like Lloyd George upon a triangle this House now is dancing a quadrille with four parties in it. Or to put it another way we have on one side a party playing the fiddle, on the other side a party playing the flute, the Farmers playing the trombone, and the Labour party the big drum. [DOT]
What is going to arise out of all this? The revolution has arrived, and I want to tell my hon. friends that the greatest menace ahead of them is that this state of affairs has arrived and is present. I do not know any party in office to-day in the British dominions that is likely to go to the people that will not have a very hard time in getting back. While there has been a revolution in the British dominions in regard to the political system, a still greater revolution is pending in the United States. There never before was such political excitement in that country as there is to-day. They have there a Republican party in charge of the administration and they can do as they like. They have also a Democratic party. But they have a third party, or rather a third and fourth party, called the Insurgent party. They are made up of insurgent Democrats and insurgent Republicans, and they are the men who are forcing the situation in the United States to-day. That country is in a state of turmoil, and nobody knows what is going to happen; but if there is anything Canada ought to watch with great interest, it is to see what will occur in the election in the United States this coming year. I would not be a bit surprised to see now the present President Mr. Coolidge not taken up by his party. I centainly expect to see an altogether new man as a presidential candidate for the Democratic party; I would be less surprised if a third presidential candidate was put forward, and he might win. It is true that Theodore Roosevelt tried it and he failed, and Mr. Taft came into office and became president; but in view of what^ is going on in the United States I am asking the Canadian people and this Canadian House to watch what is happening there and to watch how this revolution is coming. It will be so surprising and far reaching that nobody can quite tell what will happen. It is well worth watching.
Let me say a word for the new party that has come into office in England. I am not going to apologise for them. I think what has happened there is one of the most promising things that has happened in a long time. Some people say that that party are Reds, Bolshevists, Communists, and they have some other names for them. The best informed man in politics today, so far as I can judge-and I am somewhat of a judge-is Ramsay MacDonald. There is not an abler man in British politics to-day, and the ablest man, from a European point of view, is his Lord Chancellor, Lord Haldane. True, he had to admit some years ago that he was indebted to Germany for his spiritual development, for his education. But I will say this for Lord Haldane, that the greatest thing to his credit in connection with the late war was that he made a fighting machine out of the British army I am now giving the testimony of the best generals in the war, that Lord Haldane made out of the then very poor army Great Britain had, the best fighting machine in the war. Ramsay MacDonald, Lord Haldane, Mr. Clynes, who

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
is now leader of the House, the Colonial Secretary, and others who are there-some might think they were men who had been picked off the street-are men of character; they are able to take care of themselves; they are the ablest men in England. The correspondence, printed yesterday or the day before, that was exchanged between the Premier of France and the Prime Minister of Great Britain, has given to the world the hope that peace will come sooner than we expect, and that there will be an adjustment and an improvement. I am going to read to the House a few lines giving the opinion of Stanley Baldwin of this much-despised Labour party in England. It is surprising in a country like Canada to many people who profess to be reformers and others who profess to have no great regard for Communists, Bolshevists, and such people, to hear what Stanley Baldwin says of the party that happens to be in office at present in England.
I should like the House to get the benefit of this. This is the speech that he made the day after he resigned office, a speech that he made to his own followers in the House. He said:
- Our great enemies of the future are not going to be the Liberals, who are moribund, but Labour, which is very much alive. You are not going to beat Labour on a policy of tranquillity, negation or sitting still. There is a vitality in Labour at present in the country, and unless we can share a vitality of that kind we shall be unable to conquer it. Now, to my mind, the strength of Labour arises from two sources.
Then he goes on.
We have in our party no lack of material. We have all over the country young men who would be eager to work with us if they felt that we were no less sincere m our outlook than the Labour party. If they do not feel that, there is nothing that is going to stop the drift to Labour of the young men in the towns. It rests with us; and I would urge very strongly that in the next two or three months, inside our party and in consultation with experts outside, we should examine in the light of the present a number of the pressing problems that have presented themselves since the war, to be examined without prejudice-problems of housing, problems of education, and, almost more important than all, problems of the relationship between master and man anc^ that, having examined these problems, we may reach conclusions which may well form part of our social policy by the time the next election comes.
That is the Labour party that Stanley Baldwin-and he is a very able man-says they have to beat there. When people go around this country and abuse these Reds and call them Socialists, Bolshevists and all that kind of thing, they should remember that these are the men who hold office to-day in England, who have taken over the business of trying to restore prosperity, at least to restore peace, to England. I repeat what I said a few moments ago, that there never before has been a correspondence exchanged in two or three letters that has given as much 
hope to the world as that fine letter written by Ramsay MacDonald to the Premier of France and the reply in an equally honourable and fair-minded way by the Premier of France.
But all this has been carried on by a government in a minority. That is the revolution and some of us do not know it. There will soon be in this country a government carried on by a minority. But how do they do it?
Is the present government not carrying on by a minority?

Yes, but the
great feature of the new system is that it is not by votes and majorities in Houses-and this is taking place all through the United States-it is by arrangements or deals by leaders of parties within the House.

By good legislation.
Mr. MACLEAN (York :	I am not disputing it; I am saying what is coming, and the members of this House and the people of this country must see it. We have seen it arrive here. When I read that statement of the leader of the Progressive party as it appeared in the press on Saturday last I came to the conclusion at once that possibly there had been some understanding. It was an honourable declaration that if they got what they wanted along Progressive lines certain things would be done. Now, that will be the same attitude in the politics of the world. There will be no longer any two-party system. Such a system does not exist here; we have four parties here, and there are three in England, while there are several in the province of Ontario. The same thing is true in the United States in the political situation that obtains there today. So that what I am saying will be of interest, if not to the members of this House, at least to the people of Canada.
Now I come to the question of redistribution, in connection with which the government promises a measure. Anyone who has been following political tendencies in this country knows, no doubt, that the revolution has come in the province of Manitoba, where they are adopting what is known as the single transferable vote. And we are to have the same thing in this House. With the Progressives behind it that principle may come into force in Canada. And what that transferable vote means hon. gentlemen will discover if they go back to the country for re-election, whenever the time may come. This alternate vote is the principle which

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
enables minorities to secure some representation: by the transfer of votes, minorities that heretofore could not enjoy representation in parliament will now have it. In cities like Montreal and Toronto various deals will be made, and under this revolutionized condition which will prevail as a result of the transferable vote no one knows who will be elected; and that is something that confronts my hon. friends on the treasury benches more particularly than it does anyone else. Now, I do not say that I am against the transferable vote. We are to have it in the next Dominion election unless something happens to prevent the principle being adopted. The revolution, I say, has come and if hon. gentlemen do not quite believe in it and are inclined to laugh, let them wait until they go to the country. There is a minority government ruling in England and only a few days ago we had a minority government in office in this country; and with the far-reaching. changes that are imminent in the United States, in the election which is going to take place there we shall no doubt have some surprises which will have some significance to ourselves and our friends and to the prospects of the country. Parliamentary institutions, I am glad to say, do not last; changes come. That is natural, and it is well that it should be so. People thought that they could relegate these things to leaders of parties and that they could ward off these changes. Now, however, the outstanding fact is that the people are supreme, for no party leader can dictate what shall be. If the people want more parties they will have them. They will have as many as they want and no man knows what he is talking about if he gets up here and says that he is not going to allow the two-party system to die, or that he thinks this or the other should be the case; the people will settle all that. .
Let me now deal with the question of the St. Lawrence waterway. There is a percentage of the people of this country who do not like the idea of the improvement of the St. Lawrence waterway. Montreal does not like it. I should think it would be of the greatest benefit to Montreal; and if that city is not satisfied with the improvement of the St. Lawrence waterway the United States will soon make them sit up and understand that the government over there will build a canal from Buffalo to New York which would make New York the absolute port of the western world. So that when the people of Montreal say they do not want to see any improvement of the St. Lawrence, tell them they had better have a care. I believe that it
is in the interest of Canada and in the interest of the United States that the St. Lawrence waterway improvement scheme should be carried out immediately, in the same way that the Panama canal project was carried out to successful completion. That undertaking was the result of an agreement. I might read a few words from Lord Charnwood's Life of Roosevelt. In 1903 Roosevelt wrote:
Panama declared itself independent and wanted to complete the Panama canal and opened negotiations with us. I had two courses open; I might have taken the matter under advisement and put it before the Senate, in which case we should have had a number of most able speeches on the subject, and they would have been going on now and the Panama canal would be in the dim future yet. We would have had a half century of discussion and perhaps the Panama canal. I preferred we should have the Panama canal first and the half century of discussion afterwards.
And the Panama canal was built, not so much by legislation as by negotiation between the two governments. The same thing is needed in this instance. My suggestion in regard to this very necessary undertaking would be to start negotiations immediately with the United States looking to an international agreement. The great thing to be done, however, is to undertake this much-needed improvement immediately. It would provide employment in certain parts of the country and it ought to be carried out at the earliest possible date. The money could all be raised. We no doubt would have to assume half of the cost and the United States half, but there would be no trouble in raising the money, with the assistance of the United States, at a low rate of interest. If that were done the work could be completed within two years and would become the great success which the Panama canal has been. While I should not like to see the hydro-electric power investments of the people of Ontario interfered with, at the same time, if the rights of the province can be safeguarded in that connection, I should be glad to see this project undertaken including the development of water powers. In that way within two years the people of New York state and the people of Ontario and Quebec would have an immense development of water power, which would bring great strength to the manufacturing industries of both countries. Therefore I am strongly in favour of our dealing with this question at an early date.
There is an insistent call for economy of administration, and I have the utmost respect for it. Already there has been a start in this direction, there have been reductions in our national expenditure; but we must insist on still more sweeping reductions, and to this end we must do as they are doing in the

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
United States, we must stop inflation. What five or seven years ago were comparatively . small retail businesses in this country have been converted into big organizations capitalized at absurdly high figures. We have, in common with the United States, an army of profiteers, men who have made immense sums of money, and they are moving heaven and earth in their effort to ensure a continuance of profiteering. They do not want to see deflation come about. But there must be deflation. We cannot keep up the cost of living, and it will have to be reduced, even if the housewives have to go on strike. Deflation must come; and there must be other economies.
Now, I am going to suggest to the government a series of economies-and no one can give a better start in this direction than the government. To begin with my home city of Toronto, we own the street railway system, but under the system of amortization it is necessary to exact a 6|-cent fare. I would suggest that the city authorities postpone the amortization of the street railway debt for a certain time and give the people a 5-cent fare. One or two examples like that will have a markedly beneficial effect on the public. Now let me suggest what the government may do in this direction. Let them put the postage back to pre-war rates; let them make a suggestion to the board of directors of our National Railway system that passenger and express rates be put back to pre-war levels; let them reduce the rates on telegrams. The great thing is to touch the sentiment of the people, and this can be accomplished in no better way than by starting the process of deflation *which I have indicated. Therefore I hope some action will be taken by this House to bring about these reductions. As an old Greek philosopher said, tc be a harpist you must play on the harp; and to touch the imagination of the people we must play in this key, we must inaugurate economies in many directions in the Civil Service, but at the same time we must establish contact with the people at points where they are vitally interested. To do this we must give them some relief in respect to postage, telegraph, express and railway rates. So my suggestion to the House is that if we really believe in economy, if we really believe in deflation, something along this line must be started in order that high prices may be cut down and profiteering be checked. The profiteers have never yet been punished. The country is full of them. Today it is overrun by a new class of profiteer- the bond security seller. I never saw so many men trying to sell bonds all over Canada as 
I see at the present time. Let the inflation in that respect cease for a while.
The vital thing is to get back to normal, and it is hard to accomplish it. When you try to get back to normal you meet with many difficulties, nevertheless you must keep on trying and finally the sun will begin to shine again. Put a little more hope into the people, give them leadership here from Ottawa, not only by economies in the Civil Service and other departments of government, but by encouraging deflation all around. We may have to still further reduce our army. I know some people will be sorry to see our volunteer service reduced, but the Great War was an absolute failure if it does not lead to a better condition of affairs in regard to military establishments.
I come now to taxation and new sources of revenue. I spoke about a revolution in politics, and I want to suggest to hon. members a revolution that is coming in regard to raising our national revenues. Hon, members will probably be surprised and inclined to laugh at first when they hear what I have to say, but I hope to convince them of the feasibility of my suggestion. There are certain things in which we have a monopoly, and I maintain that these monopolies can be used to secure a great national revenue- from some a little, from others a great deal. We have an absolute monopoly of nickel. Practically the world's supply of nickel is contained in about eight square miles near Sudbury. This enormous deposit is no doubt the result of some great geological upheaval in former days, and as far as we know it is the only deposit of its kind in the world. We own it absolutely; but what is taking place? Sir Alfred Mond and his father came to this country twenty years ago and they were the first to grab the Sudbury nickel deposit. They have been taking it ever since over to their refinery at Swansea, and they have turned out in that one refinery all the nickel produced in Europe. I have stated in this House-and I was rebuked by members of a former government for saying it-that Germany all through the war got from the Scandinavian countries all the nickel she wanted, and it all came from Canada. My authority for that statement was the result of an investigation made by a British admiral who visited all these countries. He saw that they had this immense supply of nickel, and he knew that it came from Canada. Probably most of it came from the International Nickel Company, a United States organization which controls three-quarters of the area containing these nickel deposits. We have one company

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
here, a new company, which is producing nickel. They say they have not made any money. That is probably true, but I have no doubt that they hope to make it. Nickel is one most valuable metal in the world to-day; it is sought not only for war purposes but for other purposes as well. Nickel contains an undisclosed amount of four very rare metals besides nickel itself, palladium, polonium, platinum and irridium. I have asked from time to time that the information regarding these ingredients be given in this House, but it has never been disclosed to the Canadian people. So this nickel ore has been taken out of the country by Sir Alfred Mond and his friends and smelted at Swansea, the Canadians thus getting nothing in the way of wages. And the same thing is going on in the United States: they are smelting it there and they will not tell us what is the content of the precious metals outside of nickel. As we have the sole supply we should require the payment of a reasonable tax to the people of Canada before this nickel goes out to other countries. In other words, let us make them disclose what they actually have in this ore, and let us put an export duty on it. Nickel steel is the most useful material used in connection with the automotive industry, in fact in the manufacture of every kind of steel. If nickel steel is an absolute necessity to the world and it must be produced in Canada, we can say that it shall be manufactured before it leaves the country and that if others want it they must pay an export duty on it when it goes out. That would be a wise thing to do, and I hope it will be done.
I come now to another important question, that of pulp, pulpwood and paper export. There is no reason why those in other countries who must have our pulp, pulpwood and paper-and they are largely American people-should not pay us an export duty on those materials. Canada could get a large revenue out of that pulp industry and the people of this country would get the benefit of it. Now, the people of the United States have an absolute right to make their own tariff, but I want to tell my friends the farmers down the line here that when the United States impose a prohibitive duty on Canadian wheat going into their country of 35 cents a bushel, and are getting ready to make it 50 cents, the first thing they have to do is to stand up in this House and say, "Yes, Mr. American, you can keep us out of your countiy, but if you want our pulp we are going to make you pay an export duty on it. If you do not like to do that, perhaps you will take down your prohibitive duty on our Canadian wheat." In five years
Canada will control the wheat supply of the world, and the United States and other countries will have to come to us for what they must have. So I suggest that within five years we shall be in a position to place an export duty on wheat, and that there would be no resulting disadvantage to the farmers, but, on the contrary, a benefit. So we have all these arrows in our quiver, and many others if we care to use them.
I am confident that the greatest gold producing country in the world is going to be in northern Ontario and Quebec, and there is no reason why, with the development which will take place within a comparatively few years, we should not derive an immense revenue from the export of gold. Ontario and Quebec would benefit by it very largely. It is time we began to think about these new sources of revenue, especially in view of the attitude of the United States. They are our neighbours and they have been our allies, but they are making the farmers of our West pay 35 cents in order to get a bushel of wheat into their country. Well, we should not be blamed if we said to them, "If you want our pulpwood you will have to pay an export duty on it"; then we can use some of the revenue derived from that source in the protection of our forests, the preventing of fires, the planting of trees and the maintaining of a pulpwood supply. A tax of that kind will not hurt the pulp industry of this country, although they will groan to-morrow when they hear that I have suggested that there should be such an export duty. The pulp industry is growing; the demand in the United States for Canadian paper is becoming enormous. They cannot print their papers over there unless they get pulp from outside their own country, and they have to come to Canada for it. So we cannot be blamed if we should ask them to pay an export duty on the pulp and paper that we send over, until such time as they experience a change of heart and take [DOT] down the tariff wall that they have raised up against our wheat. It may be a crime to make any suggestion as to new policy in this House, but that is a suggested new method of raising revenue.	-
Another thing I would like to see in this country is a great iron industry, and I notice that one of the papers has entered to-day upon a campaign in that direction. So far our iron ores are rather weak and hard to handle, and although we are doing some smelting in our country it does not amount to a great deal. I am going to tell the House and the country what I think is the future of the iron industry. I have been speaking

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
about revolutionary methods of various kinds; now the greatest revolution in iron smelting is about to take place, namely, the practice of smelting by electric current. We have an enormous amount of power available on the rivers of the Hudson slope, on the St. Lawrence and elsewhere. In England they are getting ready to burn their coal at the pit heads and to generate electrical current for use in their smelters in the production of iron. If we are alert, we may be producing iron by way of electrical smelters if we have sufficient quantities of ore, and I think we will have that ore in a short time. Hitherto the conditions have been rather discouraging, but I see to-day in a trade paper devoted to these subjects that there are immense stores of iron ore in our country. I leave that question there with my suggestion in regard to what I think will be a great source of revenue, and a great source of compulsion on our neighbours, if we choose to use it, to make them accord fair treatment to the farmers of the West in regard to wheat, if nothing else. I throw out that suggestion, and as I said before, watch what is going to happen in the United States in the coming election. If perchance the Democratic party come into office in the United States in this coming election-and I admit I opposed the reciprocity proposal that was made in this country some years ago-I would not be a- bit surprised if they would come forward with an entirely new trade proposal to Canada, and use that as one reason for removing this objectionable duty on Canadian wheat.
When I was talking about economy I wanted to say this: We must continue to tax luxuries in this country. If we are not taxing them enough, let us tax them more. It will give us revenue. We must also reduce the taxes on the necessities of life.
The third thing I would suggest to the House is this: I would revise the preferential privileges in the Canadian tariff, especially in regard to our sister dominions and the Mother Country. I have heard a great deal of complaint as to the effect of those preferences. I think they might be revised, and I would suggest that they be revised.
Another thing that has got to end, and nobody yet has said it in the House

it remains for me to say it-is this: One of the greatest iniquities ever perpetrated in the United States and Canada during the war was the issuing of tax-exempted bonds, which all fell into the hands of rich men. I do not know how that can be cured. It might involve a breach of contract that Canada could not be a party to, and yet the people of the United 
States and the United States congress, and they are very honourable in their legislation especially in regard to financial obligations, are going to find a way to stop these tax-exempted bonds. I suppose their issuance could be continued in this country yet. Among the economies we may effect, and in order to increase the revenues of this country, let us put an end to issuing tax-exempted bonds. I think they have ceased in the United States, but I am not sure of that. I do not suppose the rich men and the rich companies would be generous enough to make concessions to the country, but a way may be found to get rid of this condition of affairs where rich men and rich companies have millions and millions of tax-exempted bonds in their safes, and yet be fair to the bond holders and be within the law. I am not advising repudiation in any sense, but a way may be found to end that condition, and the people of the United States are trying to solve that problem to-day. We have to solve it too, and we must stop now, once for all, the issuing of tax-exempted bonds. In future any securities issued in this country will have to take the ordinary course. Municipal bonds went out by millions when the opportunity offered to put them out, and national bonds went out by hundreds of millions, all tax-exempt. Probably that was a necessity of the war, but that must continue no longer. It may have ceased, but I do not think so.
Finally, for I do not want to tire the House much longer, I am coming back to the question of bank reform in this country, and I want to tell the House frankly that when I took up this subject last week and made investigations,
I had intended to suggest the introduction of an amendment to the Address
9 a.m. that I thought under the circumstances that existed last week this government would be prepared to accept, but since I have observed what has taken place within the last week, and the certainty almost of the government having the co-operation of my friends from the West, especially if my friends from the West are to get some of the things they desire, I saw it was not quite a wise thing to do, and accordingly I did not draft the amendment, but I am going to tell the House what I propose. What I want to see in this country is the reform of our banking system; it has to come right away, and if the government do not bring it about they will soon hear from the people. I suggest that we should substitute a national or Dominion note issue in place of the bank notes issued in this country. I suggest an absolute withdrawal of the bank notes issued by the banks and the

The Address

Mr. Maclean (York)
substitution therefor of national notes like they have in the United States. I would also suggest that we have what they have in the United States, a Federal Reserve banking system, which is a system of re-discounting for the banks. I have no hostility against the banks in this country at all. I would like to see them increase in number and their capital multiplied, four or ten times for that matter. I would like to see their business increase and the service they can give to the Canadian people increase. There are all kinds of opportunities for the banks to make money in this country, but they have got to sit down with parliament and consent to withdraw their own notes and to substitute therefor national notes. They must also be willing to accept a system of re-discounting for banks, under the same plan that obtains in the United States. Not to weary the House I am going to ask permission to read three short paragraphs I have here, written by a Canadian, as to what occurred in the United States and brought about the reform of their currency law. They are taken from an article on "Woodrow Wilson and his domestic policy." Woodrow Wilson made the greatest record of any man who was in the war. He died the other day but he hoped to bring about the League of Nations. The United States is not yet a party to the League of Nations. For some reason they repudiated their President in regard to that matter but they are coming back to it, and if I correctly interpret what Ramsay MacDonald said in the correspondence that was published a day or two ago the United States will yet come back to the League of Nations. Now let me read what I have here on Woodrow Wilson's domestic policy:
Mr. Wilson came to the White House at a time when all signs foreboded economic disturbance and distress. The Payne-Aldrich tariff law had caused agricultural depression and an equal price level similar to conditions now prevailing in many states as a result of the Fordney-McCumber tariff act. The currency of the country was inelastic with business often demoralized by "currency famines" and "money comers." The credits of the country were absolutely controlled by the private corporations in charge of the reserve banks.
The Wilson administration within a few months created the Federal Reserve Bank system, which brought the credit of the country to the relief of business and provided an elastic currency under government control. This was accompanied by a downward revision of the tariff and followed later on by a rural credit system which has already financed farm mortgage loans to the extent of a billion dollars at a moderate rate of interest and on easy terms of payment.
Had it not been for the Federal Reserve Bank it would have been impossible to finance the great orders for munitions placed by the Allies in the United States before the entrance of that country into the world war, or to have financed the huge expenditures and commitments of the Federal government after America's entrance into the war. There are many who believe that the Federal Reserve Bank system contributed no less toward the winning of the war than did the armed forces sent by America oversea.
Now, that is the American Reserve Bank sj'stem, which is based on national notes and only on national notes, which discounts for all the banks, and which supplied all the money necessary to carry on all those contracts during the war. That system is still in existence there, and they mean to keep it. We in Canada must have not only a national system of currency, but a national reserve bank system such as they have in the United States. We must start to have it this session, and the government will be tried by nothing so much as by what they endeavour to do to meet the views of the farmers. I want to tell them that unless they give the farmers a national note system in place of a bank note system, and unless they give them a national reserve bank) there will be very serious criticism. I want to read just one more paragraph about Woodrow Wilson:
Be that as it may, the Federal Reserve Bank will permanently remain the cornerstone of national finance. The Land Bank system for rural credits will also be a permanent institution.
I want my friends the farmers to note this:
Had Mr. Wilson been able to give more attention to domestic affairs he would have completed his financial programme by establishing a banking system designed to give the farmers of the country the banking accommodations given by the Federal Reserve system to merchants and manufacturers.
That is what we want in this country. We want a national system of banking that will meet the requirements of the farmers and we will not get it from the present banks. In this country there has got to be a great system of national banking, similar to what they have in the United States, for the accommodation of manufacturers and farmers. Let there be equality of treatment. The farmers today are declaring that their great grievance is lack of equality in price levels. There have been low price levels for the farmers, and a high price level for the other people engaged in industry. The same thing obtains in the matter of banking accommodation; there is discrimination. We in this country have an opportunity now to get this relief; to establish a system of national notes and a system of national reserve banks, and the latter will serve the farmers as well as the men who are engaged in commerce and in manufacturing.
I want to see a real reform in banking. The people of Canada have been deprived of the finest national savings banks they ever had. A few years ago the Receiver General's

The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
offices in Canada took deposits and gave the people interest on them, and that money was absolutely secure. Somebody strangled those offices throughout almost the whole of Canada. I am informed, and I think correctly, that the Canadian government is still carrying on this national savings bank for the benefit of the people and paying interest on deposits, in the Maritime provinces and in British Columbia. Unfortunately somebody strangled the operation of the Receiver General's office in Toronto, although it was the finest bank we ever had. The people could go into the Receiver General's office, deposit their money, draw interest on it and get that money whenever they wanted it. That change was not made by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and I do not know what minister in the former government did it. However it was done and the people of Canada, especially in the province of Ontario, have been deprived of this fine savings bank system. I want to see that national savings bank restored immediately as security for the people who entertain some doubt in regard to their bank deposits.
There is another thing I want to see carried out, and I am going to put the matter up to the government now. We must modernize our savings banks in connection with our post offices. Nobody who has a, deposit in one of these banks can get his money when he wants it. He has to sign a form * which must be sent on to Ottawa and checked up, and it is a week or more before he gets his money. I want to see the Canadian people given the right to get their money whenever they want it, not in the form of currency but a cheque which will be cashed by any bank. The people want a return to the savings bank system we formerly had in this country; they want the right to deposit their savings in a bank controlled by the government. The Drury government in Ontario did one good thing when they established what they called Ontario government savings offices. They took in millions of deposits there and those savings offices are in existence yet. The present provincial gov-vemment is talking about winding up that system, but I would advise Mr. Ferguson not to do that until he sees whether the Dominion government will not revive the system of national savings banks that obtained in connection with the Receiver General's offices, representing the treasury of this country.
And now I want to say another thing as to what is going on in the United States. The government of that country to-day are paying 
anybody 5 per cent on any deposit he likes to make with them. And they pay him immediately in the best money in the world, in national notes of the United States. During the war, and since, this system has gradually become, by reason of the improvements introduced by Woodrow Wilson, a splendid one. The finest banking system in the world to-day is in the United States. It is based on national notes, it will rediscount to the banks, it will take money on deposit from anybody in the country, and interest to the amount of 5 per cent is paid. The system has been such a success that it is making the banks over there somewhat concerned.
I want to conclude by making [DOT] another quotation. I thought I had the letter here but I cannot put my hand on it for the moment. However, I may say that I received a letter from a gentlemen for whom I have great respect. He knows all about the losses that have occurred in this country in connection with the Home Bank. I want to tell the House what he says:	The absolute
fraud	in connection with the	present
Bank Act of Canada is that the deposits in a wrecked bank are first grabbed to pay for the note issue of that bank. For that reason this parliament must do something for the people who have that grievance against the Bank Act of Canada. I do not know whether they can make out a case or not; but that is the point, that millions of the depositors' money in the Home Bank are to-day going to discharge the notes issued by that bank. This has occurred in a great number of cases in the past, and it must be cured. I wish the acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) was here; I would put the question straight to him now:	Does he intend to stop
that kind of business in this country, that when money is deposited by people in a bank, the first grab that is made on that money when trouble comes to the bank is to take up the bank notes that have been issued by that bank? That is what we are up against, and we all have to _ face depositors in that bank. We get letters every day about the matter.
The province of Quebec has had two troubles of that kind, the Provincial Bank and La Banque Nationale. It also had a good deal of trouble from a company known as La Machine Agricole, and an immense amount of securities was floated amongst the innocent people of Quebec and other parts of this country. For some reason or another Quebec has undertaken to issue $15,000,000 of the bonds of the province to take care of the people that lost their money in those bad securities and
The Address-Mr. Maclean (York)
the people who lost their money in those two banks. I want to say to the depositors in the Home Bank that they have a good reason to present to this government why something should be done for their relief, in that the province of Quebec has come to the relief of its own people who have suffered to the extent of $15,000,000 in those banks and the company by which so much money was extracted from the people of that province. It may, perhaps, be an unfair thing to ask of the government; but some consideration must be paid to the people of this country, and first of all some consideration must be paid to the reforming of. the banking laws, as I pointed out tonight. This sort of thing must stop. Why should we have any more bank notes in this country when we can get good, clean national notes such as we have? Is there any note so good in Canada to-day as the one dollar bill or the two dollar bill? It goes everywhere and every American will take such bills; but the minute you offer them a five dollar bill and they see that it is a travelling photograph album of the man who happens to be general manager or president of the bank, they will not take it.
There is another matter and, perhaps, the House and the government are not aware of it. The greatest crime is this: We have a national issue of notes and we issue notes of $5,000 and $10,000. The banks get them-I know they get them-and they go and deposit them in a central gold reserve in Montreal. Having deposited them there, they go out and reissue their own notes in the place of their national notes. They humiliate the national note, your note, the note of your nation, by saying that it is a discredited thing. Eventually the money has to be paid; but their notes go out, and that is the security that the depositor has, when the best note in the world, a note issued on the credit of the people, a note that would have gone everywhere, has its place taken by this bank note. That is taking place every day. Is the Minister of Finance going to stop it? Would it not be a good thing for our people to have a five dollar bill, or a ten dollar bill, or a hundred dollar bill, or a five thousand dollar bill of the government of Canada? But you cannot get them. We have issued them; but the banks have them all: the banks have silenced them, and in place of them they have issued their own notes. That is what the depositors in our banks have to take when they come to get their money.
I am going to conclude by just referring to this condition in regard to the banks. I have
6i
no hostility towards the banks. I want to see them make money, to prosper; but I want to see them give an absolutely secured service to the people of this country who are not getting it now. In the United States they have the finest system of national notes, the finest system of bank rediscount. They are taking the deposits of the people and they are giving them 5 per cent. If you are a depositor and 3rou want to secure your money in this country-and again I say I am sorry the acting Minister of Finance is not present- if you are doubtful about your bank deposits in this country, all you have to do is to go and deposit them in the United States, and you will actually get the security of the United States that when you want that money you will get it and you do not have to take the note of a bank that may not be able to pay its way. There are millions of securities held by the ban,ks even in this country, but there are millions of bank notes out that might be questioned any day, and unless the government is not careful to preserve the standing of such issues, in view of those things that are taking place and those revolutions that are going on, I do not know what will happen.
I want to tell the Prime Minister that if he does not consider this bank situation, his sojourn in the land of promise will not be very long. He is in the land of promise now. The Farmers have come to his relief; they have taken him on trial, and they are going to give him a close examination. They will check up the delivery of the goods every night. I do not know who the checker up is, but he will be an important man in the Progressive party. He will check up every night to see if the goods have been delivered, and if they are not delivered, something will happen. In the meantime, I would suggest that the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance should take up the banking reforms that are called for in Canada. They thought they had accomplished something last year when they put through the Bank Act. They did something, but they did not do enough. No bank should object to inspection. While I am speaking of inspection, I want to mention another thing that obtains in the United States where they have these good things. Under their National Reserve Bank system every bank must be what is called a "member bank," and that practically submits them to the inspection and criticism of their fellow members. There is thus the most careful system of banking in the United States there ever was in any country. That being the case, we should follow it. We are following

I apologise to the House for taking up its time to-night. In the short speech which I have made to-night, I have endeavoured to bring to the attention of this House and still more of the people of Canada the need there is for a greater exercise of economy from the bottom up, and the still greater reason why we should not only talk about economy but begin to practise it in this House. The government should practise it in regard to not only the Civil Service, but many other things, and it should endeavour to secure the relief I have outlined to-night in regard to postage, telegraph charges, radway fares and things of that description.
Let us just show a disposition in parliament to set an example of economy; let us deflate the awful wind that is in so many of the commercial organizations of the country; let us economise in every direction wherever economy is practicable. There is a new element in the electorate of the country to-day, and that is the woman's vote. It is getting to be equal to that of the men. In England every woman of thirty may vote. They are claiming the right to vote at the age of twenty-one and they ought to have that right. We have the woman's vote to consider in this country and at the next election, under the transferable vote system, no one knows what is likely to happen. If we do not get up on our toes and show some consideration for some of the matters I have brought to the attention of the House, I think it will go very hard with some of the politicians who may then be appealing to the country. The day of absolute majorities in deliberative assemblies has gone by. Parliaments and legislative bodies generally will now be composed of different groups, and these parties will make deals just in the same way as they have done in the United States. Over there they are carrying out great economy involving hundreds of millions, and it is being made possible by arrangement between the leaders of the different parties. I do not call such an arrangement dishonest, but the fact remains that this is just what is being done. Arrangements of this kind are prevalent in the provinces and elsewhere, and we may see surprising things now that the political revolution has come. Let no one tell me that because we have a political revolution we shall have disaster. It is the will of the people in any event, and this is a democratic country. I have always been a democrat and I am a democrat to-day. A Conservative can be a good democrat, especially in relation to

the policies that prevail here; and so can a Liberal. The day of democracy has arrived, and when hon. gentlemen go to the country for re-election they had better see to it that their compass is adjusted in keeping with the change that has taken place.

It is
with a great deal of pleasure that I have listened to the interesting address delivered by the hon. member who has just sat down (Mr. Maclean, York). I cannot say that I altogether agree with his pessimism or with the novel way in which he wishes to raise taxation. However, he has suddenly opened my eyes to one thing. I have often wondered why so many people went to the United States; now I know. I have heard a splendid eulogy of the different systems that prevail to the south, and apparently, in comparison with Canada, they are much superior to our own. Of course, in that respect I do not agree with the hon. gentleman, but I do think that some of the things that he has said are worthy of our attention, especially in regard to some of the means of raising revenue for the country. I do not think that the hon gentleman's prophecy concerning wheat in Canada in five years' time will come true. We all know that Russia, that great agricultural country of Europe and Asia, is steadily coming back and always will be a great factor in the world's market for wheat. For that reason I do not think that the time will ever come in Canada when we shall have a complete monopoly of the situation and be able to charge just what we please for our commodity. I do think, however, in view of the situation in Canada, that it might be necessary to prevent the export of pulpwood to the nation to the south of us. I am speaking entirely for myself in this matter.
You are becoming a protectionist.

Not at all; but I remember
coming to this country twenty-one years ago and taking particular observation of the great forests I passed through in going to the West; and during the past few years, coming to Ottawa and going back again, I have been comparing my recent observations with those of twent5r-one years ago and I find that all along the railway tracks those great forests have been depleted, not only by those who have gone in to cut wood but also by forest fires. It seems to me, when we talk about our vast resources and their development and about utilizing them to our own advantage, that these resources belong not only to us but to our children and our children's children,

The Address-Mr. Lewis
and there should be some method of safeguarding the great forests we have in Canada for the generations that are to come. I therefore consider it quite legitimate that we should put an export duty on the large amount of pulpwood that is going to the United States at the present time. In my opinion there is a great deal of waste, both in the United States and in Canada, in the use of paper. One may pick up a weekly newspaper and see sometimes from thirty-six to perhaps seventy pages which, so far as the items of real news interest are concerned, might very well be condensed into six or seven pages. Instead, about seventy pages are wasted, and that means a tremendous inroad into a great national heritage which has been given us by Providence. An export duty on pulp-wood would possibly remedy this wastefulness which is taking place to-day.

Now, Mr. Speaker, I listened yesterday with a great deal of interest to the speeches both of the leader of the government (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and frankly, to say the least, 1 was quite disappointed, not with regard to the manner in which those speeches were delivered nor altogether from the standpoint of their subject matter or the outlook which both hon. gentlemen had upon the Dominion at large; but I was disappointed to know that it was possible for such conditions to have existed in the party politics of this country. I can quite understand that if the revelations were even partially true the extravagance of the past has to a large extent been the means of bringing the Dominion into its present situation. I believe the time has arrived when great national leaders should not, as it were, be washing the dirty linen of party politics, and that in the present national crisis we should have from them speeches outlining great reforms, somewhat similar to what we may observe in Great Britain at the present time, speeches presenting solutions of the problems which confront our people, and so help to bring about that peace which is the rightful heritage of this wonderful land.
My leader has very adequately covered the whole situation in regard to the Progressive viewpoint, and therefore it will not be necessary for me to enter into any details with respect to the subjects he dealt with, although I do wish to speak on some of the problems confronting us in the West. I think our leader is to be congratulated on the comprehensive manner in which he discussed the
situation I also admired the candour and courage of the member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), who very often stands alone but is not afraid to voice his convictions, and who it seems to me, stands out sometimes like a prophet of old and reveals conditions as he finds them in our national life.
I think the Speech from the Throne is the best that I have heard since I became a member of this House. It is comprehensive in its treatment, and I think it truly describes the conditions obtaining to-day in this country. I was glad to find the subject of tariff reduction mentioned. It is, of course, a subject on which everyone can speak, to a certain extent, with ease, but I wish to say to my constituents at home and to the people of Canada generally that I do not believe that even tariff reductions are a panacea for all the ills from which we are suffering, although it is a step in the right direction. I was pleased to note that there would probably be a reduction of the tariff on implements. It may be true that certain of our implement manufacturers have lost a great deal of money and have gone out of business; but it is also true that thousands of farmers, who also had large investments in land and equipment, have been similarly unfortunate and lost all their capital, and there is no reason why fifty-two per cent of our population should be made to suffer for the sake of a few.
But it seems to me that the manufacturers have aiready anticipated the promised tariff reduction, because long before I came East it was stated by the imp'ement agents in the West that the prices of implements had gone up at least ten per cent. Even if the government were to place agricultural implements on the free list the price to the farmer would be just the same as heretofore unless the dumping clause is repealed.
Of course, this tariff reduction will remove a grievance which the West has had against the East, and this in itself is I think a splendid thing. It has always been a grouch with the western farmer, a grouch which has always troubled the Liberal or any other party in the West, and the removal of this grievance will go a long way to bring the people together in that national unity which we so much desire.
With regard to the economic outlook in the West, it is quite true, and nobody in this part of the House wishes to deny it, that we have had the most bountiful crops. Providence has helped to solve the problem of removing our difficulties. And if it could be

The Address[DOT]-Mr. Lewis
said of the government and of the capitalistic interests that they had done their share to that end we would be considerably nearer that prosperity which is so desirable. But when we as a people compare the prices in the reports that come to us from Ottawa, which show that so far as the farmers' commodities are concerned the ratio between what we sell and what we buy is 100 to 159 per cent, treating 100 as the basis before the war. If' it was difficult for the farmer to make a profitable living before the war on a 100 to 100 per cent basis, it will be readily seen how impossible it is for him to do so when the basis is 100 to 159 per cent. So, for that reason, some means must be devised whereby this discrepancy can be removed and prices of commodities which we have to purchase brought down to the pre-war basis if we are to become prosperous or even to remain on the land.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) mentioned that as a result of the failure of the wheat board legislation we were endeavoring to form a wheat pool to market our wheat. This is quite true, and a great many people believe that it will help us considerably, but I do not think we should be too sanguine of the results that may be obtained. We may be able to save a few cents by this method, but when we come to scan the world's economic and industrial position at the present time it appears to be impossible for us to raise the price of wheat in the world's market to any great extent. Take the position of Great Britain to-day; she buys the largest amount of our grain. At the present time her industries are almost at a standstill. It is reported that on the Clyde where sixty great shipbuilding yards used to employ over 96,000 people, today only about one-half of the yards are in operation with only one-third of the men in employment. As the result of the nonrecovery of Europe Great Britain's manufacturing output to-day is not 50 per cent of what it was in pre-war times. So just as long as we have these conditions in Europe we cannot expect to increase the world's market price of grain. Therefore the solution for our troubles is not to be found in that direction. Pending the recovery of Europe, which will take a long time, there is something that Canada can do, and it is this I wish to emphasize to-night. I remember reading a statement which was supposed to have been made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). Dealing with the much-needed branch lines in the West- of which I shall speak later-I understand ^Mr. Lewis.]
that he said in Moose Jaw, referring to the Senate:	We are waiting for the Lord to
reform the Senate by death, but He has not been working very hard. I do not think it is much good waiting for Providence to solve all our problems; we ought to be able to take some steps ourselves towards their solution. When we go into the costs of production we find that in the case of the farmer these costs are too great.
When I was coming down to the opening of the provincial legislature in Regina, I happened to meet one of the members there. He did not know me, and he did not know I knew him, and began to speak of the farming situation in this country. He said something like this:	It is not the fault of the government or of our present system; it is due to the false position of the farmer on the land. It is impossible, he contended, for any man with a family to moke the farm pay if he goes on in the way that he does at present. Thirty or forty years ago in Ontario we lived on the farm; we never went to the town; we manufactured all our own things; and he had come to the conclusion that no Britisher, no Canadian, could really live on the farm and that the best thing to do would be to get people from Europe who could go on the land and stay there, who would never go to the town or to a picture show. Well, if that is the real economic foundation of living on the farm to-day, then I say that it is far better for us as a nation to go out of agriculture. But I believe that it is possible to live on the farm and have a comfortable existence if the conditions are made right. The first thing I would emphasize is the necessity for a reduction in freight rates. I do not see why it should not be provided in legislation that from the time the farmer places his grain on the car until it reaches the point nearest its destination it should not be interfered with, thus avoiding a great many charges, and if that is done there is no reason why the freight rate should not be lowered.
It was pointed out by my leader (Mr. Forke) that there should be a revaluation of the railways. We shall never make the Canadian National Railways pay on the basis of the purchase price. I have for two years urged in this House that this be done, and I believe it is the only business procedure to follow. Let us revalue the lines, put them on a business basis, and then I am confident that in competition with the Canadian Pacific or any other railway we can carry the farmers' wheat much cheaper than we are doing at the present time.

The Address-Mr. Lewis
A few months ago some of the farmers in my district decided to send a car of turkeys to Toronto. I understand that a car of coal can be sent from Alberta to Toronto for $400, yet when they shipped that carload of turkeys and sent a man along with them it cost in the neighbourhood of $1,200. Why the discrimination? As long as conditions of this kind exist we shall never be able to make farming pay.
Just here I would like to say a word in regard to diversified farming, as it is called. How many of our farmers would succeed under present market conditions if they all went into diversified farming? I have spoken to the dean of the University of Saskatchewan on this subject, and he expresses the view that diversified farming is our only salvation. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has gone all over the country and he tells us the same thing; he can point to men in almost every district who have gone into this kind of farming and have succeeded in greater or less degree. But if every farmer in the district attempts to do the same thing, what is the result? Why, there is no market. Let me give you an instance: The cry was raised that we should go into the raising of chickens, turkeys, and so on; the year after some of the women on the farms did go into it and they got 25 to 35 cents a pound for their poultry. This year nearly every farmer's wife in the district did her best to raise turkeys, and the result was that some of them got as low as 11 cents a pound. If a breast bone happened to be a little crooked, 5 cents a pound was taken off; if in killing the bird they broke the wing, it went by default; anyway, the farmer got nothing for it. I do not know who got it. Now, I am not running farming down, but I want to show you the conditions. In our district we decided that we would give $5 to different high school boys who would stay on the farm and show how much they could make with it. I know one boy who with his $5 bought three ducks, one drake and a dollar's worth of food. He was able to raise thirty-four number one prime ducks. He looked after them the whole year, then he made a box and shipped them down to Pat Burns; and in return for all his work he got the magnificent sum of $2.90 over and above the purchase price. Do you think you are going to interest educate4 boys on any basis of that kind? These /ittle instances may not amount to much but they impress our educated youths and cause them to decide to divert their energies into some more profitable channel. Therefore I would impress upon the government the need for reducing the costs of production. I may point out that I have one instance where, of
the total sum received for a number of turkeys, the commission man got one-quarter, freight consumed one half, and the man who raised them got the other quarter. How can we continue diversified farming under conditions such as these? I believe the time is coming when the great leaders in Canada should get together, and, not in the spirit of party politics, a spirit which was displayed here last night; not in revealing terrible conditions as we heard them revealed, but with the interests of the people only in view, should sit down and devote their best abilities to arriving at some solution of our problems which will have the effect of bringing about contentment and prosperity.
I believe that the development of any important outlet for our grain and other commodities should receive attention, and I am of the opinion that the Vancouver harbour improvements, which have received a great deal of support from this government, will be highly beneficial to the West. I would like to mention also in passing that the Hudson Bay railway is a necessity. Of course we do not know whether or not it will be a success, but there is one thing that I think the western people deserve: they have been promised this railway and until it is tried out in actual experience no one in this House has any right to say that it will be a failure, I believe that the Hudson Bay railway will be one of the greatest benefits to our farmers in the West.
In regard to this question of diversified farming, I have an article which has some bearing upon the subject. We know that the embargo has been lifted from the export of cattle from this country to England. What price do we get for the finest quality beef at the present time? Three and four cents, and under present conditions it is not being raised at a profit, and any profit we might have on the British market has been swallowed up by the steamship companies. I do not see why this thing cannot be broken. Why, I understand the cost has been raised from $15 to $25 per head. It has been said by a notable authority that cattle can be carried overseas at $10 per head. The difference between $10 and $25 would make all the difference in the world to the cattle raisers in the West, and I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), who claims that he has the western situation at heart, should see to it and by every means in his power endeavour to break that monopoly which seems to exist in the shipping industry at the present time. I do not like to call down our merchant marine. It cost $70,000,000 of the Canadian people's money, but if we cannot break the

The Address-Mr. Lewis
combine in any other way, let these vessels be converted and be put on the ocean, and let us show to the world that these cattle can be carried overseas at the minimum rate per head. That is the only way I think in which we can solve some of the difficulties.
Now I want to speak for a moment or two in regard to the branch lines. I understand that the government is bringing down once again this year the three-year programme. I do not think this government has any right to prejudice the case of the branch lines in the West or in the East by bringing down a programme which they know will possibly not pass the Senate. The Senate has been blamed for a great many things. Possibly the Senate did right last year in stopping the programme of three years. We have in this parliament eveiy year an estimate for the Welland canal, for instance. It was estimated in the first place that the Welland canal would cost possibly $70,000,000. That estimate was later increased and I was told by one of the ministers that it might reach the sum of $100,000,000, but the government has never so far come to parliament and asked us to pass $100,000,000 to cover the work over a series of years on the Welland canal. They have asked us to pass eight or seven or eleven million dollars from year to year for the maximum amount of work that can be carried on that year. Why cannot we deal with the branch lines in the same way? Let the government come down with an appropriation in the railway estimates for branch lines and ask for a sufficient amount to carry on the maximum amount of work that can be done this year. I am quite sure that if that were done this parliament, every part of it, would vote the money gladly, and even though it may take three years to finish the work once it is begun, there is no reason why this parliament should not vote from year to year sufficient money to carry on the programme. For that reason I sincerely hope that instead of prejudicing the case by bringing forward a three-year programme, or trying to reform the Senate if it needs reforming, the government will bring in a programme for one year that will appeal not only to members of the House but to members of the Senate as being constitutional in procedure, and then I believe that the West and the East will get our much needed railways. I have a little clipping here in which the hon. Minister of Agriculture throws the whole blame upon the Senate. He may be correct in his judgment, but at the same time I hope there will be no failure this year, and that the much needed branch lines in the West and in the East will not be pre-
judiced by unconstitutional, if it is unconstitutional, procedure.
We heard a great deal last night in regard to our national outlook, in regard to the burdens of our country which to a large extent are post-war in their nature,
10 p.m. but any student of the great war and of subsequent history will admit that Canada has been very fortunate and that we have passed through the reconstruction period possibly better than any other country in the British Empire. I look with a great deal of optimism to the future. I do not see why we who have been more fortunate than any other country in the British Empire in that respect should be pessimistic in regard to the ultimate lifting of the great burden of taxation on the people. It is stated that we have a huge national debt, but should we despair when that debt is smaller than that of any other country in the British Empire? The national debt of Canada, per capita, is $270.12, as compared with $359.60 for Australia, $811.90 for New Zealand, $533.05 for South Africa, and approximately $850 for Great Britain. Why if il is possible for Ramsay MacDonald to look forward with hope and optimism to solving the problem in Great Britain where the national debt per capita is almost four times greater than our own, is it not possible for our public men with their brains and capacity and their national love for Canada to solve a much less problem? I believe that it can be done, and I hope that the best men of the nation will get together and see to it that nothing shall stand in the way-no political party, no interference of any kind. Let the solving of that problem become one of the greatest issues before this parliament at the present time.
In conclusion, I just wish to say a few words in regard to immigration. Last year I spoke at length on the Immigration Bill that passed through the House, and I think I took a very moderate attitude at that time. I want to say that as far as my own municipality and my own constituency are concerned, we need men to fill up the gaps made by those who have left. I went to the clerk of my municipality before coming down here. We had a splendid crop and I asked him, "What is the auditor's report in regard to the residents of this municipality?" He said, "There are eighty less residents than we had last year." Eighty less residents in that one municipality. That is very disheartening in regard to schools, in regard to churches, in regard to the village life and the social life of the community. We must change these

Privilege-Mr. Macdonald, (Pictou)
conditions so that our men, the finest brawn that can be found possibly anywhere in the world, can stay and live at home with us. I believe that these men are superior in every way to any people you can bring into this country, I do not care where they come frcm, and the people who live here and belong to this country have the right to the first consideration on the part of any government in this country. I trust that these vacant places will be filled up in such a way that our schools and our churches and our village life will go on in the way it has been going on in the past. I hate to see great stretches of our country devastated as a result of people leaving us and though I believe that as a result of the good crop the people are in much better circumstances than before, having received the benefit of the crop, yet a great many of them were so deeply in debt that they saw no way of recovering themselves and many moved out while they had the opportunity and while the going was good. I believe that so far as the farmer is concerned, although he may not have more money at the present time, he has paid some of his back debts. But what I do say is this, that our bank collectors and other collectors have been on the scene ever since the noise of a good crop went out, and they have collected almost to the last farthir.g, and they have left the farmer in some instances in pretty poor circumstances. But with a continuance of good crops and a continuation of the good treatment of the people by Providence we may be able, in the course of a number of years, to overcome the existing situation. I think the problem can be solved much more quickly than by merely waiting for the effect of good crops. We can remove the drawbacks that are detrimental to the great basic industry of our national life. But acompaning this there must be prudent action in our homes, in our villages, in our municipalities, and in our governments provincial and federal. There must be mutual co-operation between the people and their representatives in the direction of helping to bring about a reduction in the cost of living and a return of peace, happiness and prosperity is assured to this great Dominion.
